terms.def: The area with a 1% or higher chance of flooding in any given year.

The 25 foot rule applies to an existing zoning lot split between two or more zoning districts that permit different uses or have different bulk rules (C1-9 and R8B, for example). When the width of one district measures 25 feet or less at every point, the use and bulk regulations of the larger district can be applied to the entire zoning lot.

New York City's phone number for government information and services, answered 24 hours a day, seven days a week, in over 170 languages. Tenants use 311 (or 311Online and the mobile app) to file housing complaints, which 311 sends to the proper agency, such as HPD.

A property tax exemption program for new residential construction tied to affordability requirements. Originally created in 1971. Expired in June 2022. Successor legislation has been debated but not enacted as of 2025.
A limited loan program HPD offers in some 7A buildings to repair or replace major systems or make other repairs.

A program under New York State law in which a court appoints an administrator to run a privately owned building with conditions dangerous to tenants' life, health and safety. The administrator collects rents to pay for essential services and repairs. HPD monitors 7A administrators.

terms.term: A Policy on Geometric Design of Highways and Streets
terms.def: An AASHTO publication, often called the "Green Book," containing design practices in universal use as the standard for highway geometric design.

A permit from the Asbestos Technical Review Unit, run jointly by DEP and DOB. An owner must file a Workplace Safety Plan with DEP and get it when asbestos abatement will compromise fire protection or safety systems.

terms.term: AASHTO (American Association of State Highway Transportation Officials)
terms.def: A nonprofit, nonpartisan association representing highway and transportation departments in the fifty states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico, across air, highways, public transportation, rail and water. It publishes design guidance including A Policy on Geometric Design of Highways and Streets (the "Green Book").
Administrative Code: an abbreviation DOB uses for a law, code or policy document, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Administrative Code: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

Designing and building so people with physical disabilities can use a building, following the federal ADA Standards, HUD rules, Building Code Chapter 11 and Appendices E, N and P, and/or ICC/ANSI A117.1.
A sign that promotes a business, product or service on the same zoning lot, such as a sign above a pizza shop.

An accessory use is a use that is incidental to and customarily found in connection with the principal use. An accessory use must be conducted on the same zoning lot as the principal use to which it is related, unless the district regulations permit another location for the accessory use. (Off-site accessory parking facilities, for example, are permitted in certain zoning districts.)

The federal law giving civil rights protections to people with disabilities, similar to protections based on race, color, sex, national origin, age and religion. It guarantees equal opportunity in public accommodations, employment, transportation, state and local government services, and telecommunications.
The full City Council voted to pass the item. A bill for a local law then goes to the Mayor; a resolution takes effect on the Council's vote alone.
The average number of vehicles passing a point or using a roadway per day: total traffic volume over a period (in whole days) divided by the number of days. Sometimes called VPD (Vehicles Per Day).

A commercial business such as an adult bookstore, adult-only eating or drinking place or adult theater (or a combination) that regularly features sexually explicit films or images. Some also offer live entertainment where patrons are exposed to specified anatomical areas of the staff.

A sign that promotes a business, product or service located off the zoning lot, such as a billboard. Allowed in Manufacturing Districts but may not light up or flash there; generally restricted in Residence Districts.
A sworn, signed statement that some condition has been met. The signer is legally accountable if the statement later proves false and the condition was not met.
When the cost of living meets people's needs, so residents can stay in the city and succeed.

Housing where costs (rent or purchase price) are restricted based on income. Generally defined as costing no more than 30% of a household's gross income. NYC uses AMI thresholds to define affordability levels across different programs.
After Hours Variance: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

The unused floor area permitted on a zoning lot beyond what is already built. In some circumstances, those unused development rights may be transferred to another lot, often to allow a neighboring property to build larger than its own zoning would otherwise permit.
Alteration: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Alteration Type 1: a DOB building/job type code, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Alteration Type 2: a DOB building/job type code, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Alteration Type 3: a DOB building/job type code, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

A project that always results in a new or amended Certificate of Occupancy. It may involve a substantial enlargement or reduction of the building, or a major change to its entrance or exit, zoning use group and/or Building Code occupancy.

The kind of change in use or structure to an existing building that needs a DOB permit. There are three types, from more to less change: Alteration-1 (Alt-1), Alteration-2 (Alt-2) and Alteration-3 (Alt-3).

An HPD enhanced enforcement program that selects 250 distressed multiple dwellings each year. It can impose fees, issue Orders to Correct, and replace building systems if the owner fails to act. Owners and tenants are notified if their building is selected (selection on January 31).

A change to a permit after it was first approved, which requires filing an amendment application. Changes often arise during construction as new information comes up and need a Post-Approval Amendment.

Using proper fasteners to support and secure structural members (wall, column, deck, post or beam), fixtures and equipment. Anything supported by an exterior wall must be positively anchored to the main structure and designed for vertical and lateral loads.

Created in 2024, a small additional housing unit allowed on a lot with a one- or two-family home, such as a backyard cottage, garage conversion or basement apartment. Restrictions apply in some areas over flooding and neighborhood context. An ADU can be a permitted obstruction in a rear yard, and no parking is required for it. See ZR Section 12-10.

terms.term: Annual Notice (lead paint and window guards)
terms.def: The notice owners send tenants each January asking whether a child under six lives in or routinely spends 10 or more hours a week in the apartment, and whether a child 10 or younger lives there. Tenants must fill it out and return it.

An HPD unit that uses data to find buildings where tenant harassment may be happening, does roof-to-cellar inspections, interviews tenants, brings harassment cases in Housing Court, works with DOB, and connects tenants with legal services.
Administrative Policy and Procedure Notice: an abbreviation DOB uses for a law, code or policy document, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Status used mostly for land use matters (such as rezonings reviewed under ULURP): the Council voted in favor of the resolution approving the application.

A device that communicates pedestrian signal timing in non-visual formats such as audible tones, speech messages or vibrating surfaces. Installation in NYC is governed by the Accessible Pedestrian Signals Policy enacted October 21, 2019.
Architectural: a DOB permit type code, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Facade elements such as cornices, moldings and facade sculpture that, on older buildings, may project into the public right of way.
Hard-burnt clay, glazed or unglazed, used as cladding or veneer on exterior walls. It can be plain or ornamental, machine-extruded or hand-modeled, and is usually larger than brick or facing tile.
Arc Fault Circuit Interrupter: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

The midpoint of a region's income distribution, set annually by HUD for the New York metro area. Affordable housing programs set rents or sale prices as a percentage of AMI. 100% AMI for a family of four in NYC is roughly $130,000.
A space below grade next to a building that is open to the outside air and enclosed by walls.
The part of the roadway system serving as the principal network for through-traffic, connecting areas of major traffic generation and important highways entering the city.

The Zoning Resolution's levels of organization. Articles (Roman numerals) cover broad topics; each has up to nine chapters; chapters break into sections numbered by article and chapter, so Section 23-40 is Article II, Chapter 3, height and setback. Sections can divide into lettered paragraphs, numbered subparagraphs and romanettes.
Allowances for portions of a required street wall to project forward or recess backward, such as bay windows on townhouses, giving designers flexibility and echoing older buildings.

A proposal that complies with all applicable zoning rules and does not require discretionary approval from the City Planning Commission or Board of Standards and Appeals. As-of-right projects can proceed directly to a building permit without community board or public review.

An as-of-right development complies with all applicable zoning regulations and does not require any discretionary action by the City Planning Commission or Board of Standards and Appeals. Most developments and enlargements in the city are as-of-right.
A fiber in some building materials, such as insulation and roofing, that can cause health problems. Building owners must control it during renovations or other work by hiring special contractors.
The status in BISWeb of a plan or document that has been given to an individual agency employee to review.
Lighting fixtures and devices attached to a building facade.

An attic allowance is an increase of up to 20 percent in the maximum floor area ratio (FAR) for the provision of a pitched roof. The allowance is available in R2X districts and all R3 and R4 (except R4B) districts.

terms.term: Attic Allowance in Lower Density Growth Management Areas
terms.def: Outside of Lower Density Growth Management Areas (LDGMA), the increased floor area must be directly beneath the pitched roof and have a ceiling height between five and eight feet.
A legal review to make sure a legal form was completed truthfully or work was performed correctly.

A discretionary action by the City Planning Commission that modifies specified zoning requirements when required findings are met. Less involved than a special permit, and does not require a full ULURP vote by the City Council.
A cover over the sidewalk supported from the wall, not the ground. It needs a permit to install. See also Canopy.
A projection wholly supported by the building it is attached to, made of a lightweight frame with a covering, that provides weather protection, identity or decoration.
A device that keeps contaminated water (such as water mixed with bleach) from flowing from a business back into the NYC drinking water supply.
An above-grade extension on the outside of a building, enclosed by a wall or railing (balustrade), reached from an occupied space.
The elevation of surface water from a flood that has a 1% or higher annual chance of occurring in any given year.
The maximum permitted height of a building's street wall before any required setback. Once a building reaches its base height, it must step back from the street before continuing upward.

The base plane is a horizontal plane from which the height of a building is measured. It is utilized in most lower-density and contextual districts, and for property subject to waterfront zoning. Often, the base plane is at curb level; on sites that slope upwards or downwards from a street, or on large lots where buildings are far from a street, the base plane is adjusted to more accurately reflect the level at which the building meets the ground.

A basement is a building story that has at least one-half of its floor-to-ceiling height above curb level or the base plane. By contrast, a cellar has at least one-half of its floor-to-ceiling height below curb level or the base plane. A basement is included in floor area calculations.
Buildings Bulletin: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Building Code: an abbreviation DOB uses for a law, code or policy document, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A yearly report owners file with HPD each December on bedbug occurrences in their buildings; the filing receipt must be distributed or posted.

Rusty-red insects up to the size of apple seeds that feed on human blood but do not carry disease, spreading between apartments through cracks. HPD may use a trained dog for inspections and issues violations if live bedbugs are seen.

Every two- or three-wheeled device a person rides, propelled by human power through a belt, chain or gears, with wheels in tandem or tricycle form. It excludes devices with solid tires meant only for sidewalk use by pre-teenage children. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 102; RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))
A designated space marked with crosshatch or chevron markings that separates a bicycle facility from traffic and/or parking.

A general term for improvements and provisions made by public agencies to accommodate or encourage bicycling, including parking and storage facilities and shared roadways not specifically designated for bicycle use.

A dedicated on-street or grade-separated lane for bikes, typically delineated with markings, a curb or a parking lane within the roadway, or physically separated from the roadway for most of its length.

New multi-family residential, community facility and commercial developments must provide secure bicycle parking. Multi-family buildings need one enclosed space per two dwelling units. Bicycle parking areas are exempt from floor area, within limits.

A bikeway designated by the jurisdiction with directional and informational route markers, with or without route numbers. In NYC the Street Design Manual sets out five types: Shared Lanes, Conventional Bike Lanes, One-Way Protected Bike Lanes, Two-Way Protected Bike Lanes, and Grade-Separated Bike Lanes.

A not-for-profit corporation of property owners and commercial tenants that promotes business development and quality of life. BIDs provide supplemental services such as sanitation, maintenance, public safety, visitor services, marketing, capital improvements and beautification, funded by a special assessment paid by property owners in the district.
A generic term for any road, street, path or way specifically designated in some manner for bicycle travel, whether exclusive to bicycles or shared with other modes.
Buildings Identification Number: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

A bioswale is a landscape element designed to capture storm water run-off from adjacent surface areas. It has inverted sloped sides that allow rainwater to drain into it and contains vegetation and mulch designed to remove pollutants before the water infiltrates into the soil. They are required in certain parking lots accessory to commercial and community facility uses.
Boiler: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit), per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A block is a tract of land bounded on all sides by streets or by a combination of streets, public parks, railroad rights-of-way, pierhead lines or airport boundaries.
A blockfront is that portion of a block consisting of all of the zoning lots fronting on a single street.

The BSA, composed of five commissioners appointed by the Mayor, reviews and grants applications for special permits, as prescribed in the Zoning Resolution, for certain proposed developments and uses. The BSA also grants variances for zoning lots with irregular physical conditions where construction might not otherwise be possible. In addition, the Board hears and decides appeals to determinations by the Department of Buildings.

A short vertical post or similar structure that defines areas in the streetscape, often used to separate pedestrians or streetscape elements from vehicles. In a line, bollards keep motor vehicles out of pedestrian space such as sidewalks or plazas.
Builders Pavement Plan: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

A flexible, high-performance rapid transit mode combining physical, operating and system elements into a permanent integrated system with a distinct identity, designed to improve the speed, reliability and attractiveness of bus service. Select Bus Service is NYC's application of BRT.
Board of Standards and Appeals: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Building Schedule of Occupancy: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Between: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

A rating system, developed by the Illuminating Engineering Society (IES), describing the types of stray light escaping from an outdoor lighting fixture, making it easier to compare and evaluate outdoor luminaires.

A building is a structure that has one or more floors and a roof, is permanently affixed to the land and is bounded by open areas or the lot lines of a zoning lot. An attached building* abuts two side lot lines or is one of a row of abutting buildings. A detached building* is a freestanding building that does not abut any other building and where all sides of the building are surrounded by yards or open areas within the zoning lot. A semi-detached building* is a building that abuts or shares a wall, on a side lot line, with another building on an adjoining zoning lot and where the remaining sides of the building are surrounded by open areas or street lines. A zero lot line building* is a freestanding building that abuts one side lot line of a zoning lot and does not abut any other building on an adjoining zoning lot.
A building envelope is the maximum three-dimensional space on a zoning lot within which a structure can be built, as permitted by applicable height, setback and yard controls.
Building height refers to a building’s elevation as measured from the curb level or base plane to the roof of the building (except for permitted obstructions, such as elevator bulkheads).
A unique seven-digit number that the NYC Department of City Planning assigns to each building, used on DOB's BISWeb.
DOB's online database for any property in New York City, including violations, applications and inspections, and for registered contractors.
The uses and activities allowed in a building, as defined by the Certificate of Occupancy DOB issues for it.
A vertical extension of the exterior wall at the edge of a roof, terrace, balcony, walkway or other structure that acts as a safety barrier.

A building segment is a portion of a building where each portion has one or more dwelling units served by a separate entrance. For example, a row of attached townhouses is comprised of building segments.

Installing, modifying or upgrading building systems such as plumbing, boiler, sprinkler, standpipe, fire alarm, HVAC and fire suppression. If the work modifies these systems, the alteration's scope of work must include them.
The City agency that oversees construction and maintenance of buildings in New York City and the uses allowed in them.

The size and shape of a building as controlled by zoning regulations, including lot size, floor area ratio (FAR), lot coverage, open space, yards, height, and setback requirements. Bulk regulations determine how large and in what form a building can be built.

Rules that establish the size and shape of buildings and how a building is positioned on a property, so buildings fit their neighborhood and light and air reach the street, neighbors and occupants. Floor area, yards, lot coverage, and height and setback rules are all bulk regulations.

A bulkhead is an enclosed structure on the roof of a building that may include mechanical equipment, water tanks and roof access from interior stairwells. It is not counted as floor area and is permitted to exceed zoning height and setback requirements, within limits specified in the Zoning Resolution.

Every motor vehicle seating more than fifteen adults plus the operator and used to transport people, and every charter, interstate, intrastate, school and sightseeing bus regardless of seating capacity. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))
A street that carries one or more regularly scheduled local, commuter or intercity bus lines running on a published schedule.

An offer by an owner to pay a tenant to move out or give up their rights. Repeated buyout offers, or offers made with threats, obscene language, false information, or contact at the tenant's workplace without written permission, can be harassment.
A City law requiring owners who sign a buyout agreement with a lawful occupant to report its terms to HPD by email (buyoutagreement@hpd.nyc.gov).
Crane and Derrick: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Wages an employer must pay under State law when sending an employee home early for lack of work.

A permanent, rigid projection with a covering that provides weather protection, identity or decoration. It must be structurally independent, or attached to a building at one end and supported by at least one post (stanchion) at the outer end.
A cover over the sidewalk held up by poles fixed in the sidewalk. It requires a permit. See also Awning.

Under City Charter Section 210, a project to construct, reconstruct, acquire or install a physical public improvement classified as a capital asset (including preliminary studies and financing costs), acquisition of permanent property, initial furnishings or equipment, improvements to streets, parks, bridges, tunnels, sewers and similar infrastructure, or other projects the local finance law allows with mayoral and comptroller approval.
A beverage or liquid food container lined with plastic film to make it leak-proof (milk and soup cartons, juice boxes). Recycled with metal, glass and plastic, not with paper.
A paving material, such as concrete, that is poured into place on site and set to harden.

An exterior wall, usually masonry, with an outer and inner layer of brick (wythe) separated by a continuous air space and tied together with wire or sheet-metal ties. The air space provides insulation.
Control Access Zone: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Curb Cut: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit), per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

A cellar is a level of a building that has at least one-half of its floor-to-ceiling height below curb level or the base plane. By contrast, a basement has at least one-half of its floor-to-ceiling height above curb level or the base plane. A cellar is not included in floor area calculations.
An organization that gives New Yorkers facing foreclosure referrals to legal services, housing counseling and consumer education (646-786-0888 or 311).
Along the long dimension of a block, if the zoning map shows no boundary, the district boundary runs through the center of the block.

City Environmental Quality Review, New York City's environmental review process for discretionary actions, implementing SEQRA at the city level. CEQR assesses whether a proposed action may have significant adverse environmental impacts in areas including land use, traffic, noise, air quality, and historic resources.
Certification/Certificate/Certified: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

Approval from the Landmarks Preservation Commission that proposed exterior work on a landmarked building or property within a historic district is appropriate to the character of the landmark. CB6's Landmarks & Land Use Committee reviews CoA applications and submits an advisory recommendation before the LPC public hearing.

terms.term: Certificate of Appropriateness, Certificate of Minor Work, or Certificate of No Effect
terms.def: Formal approvals from the NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission for work on a historic building. The glossary says one is needed when the work does not need a DOB permit, whether or not it affects architectural details.
A formal document linking the name customers see (the assumed or doing-business-as name) to the business's legal name on legal documents.
A document approving a business to collect sales tax on behalf of New York State.

An LPC approval for minor work on a landmarked property or within a historic district that has no effect on the protected architectural features. Less involved than a full Certificate of Appropriateness.

A certification owners of covered buildings must get from HPD before DOB will approve certain permits involving demolition or a change in use or occupancy. HPD investigates the building's recent history and denies it if tenants were harassed. Covered buildings include single room occupancy buildings, buildings in special planning districts, and buildings selected for the Pilot Program.

A document issued by the Department of Buildings when a building is finished, verifying that it is safe to be occupied. For affordable housing under MIH or UAP, HPD must sign off on the finished units before DOB can issue the CO.

A certification is a non-discretionary action taken by the City Planning Commission, or its Chairperson, informing the Department of Buildings that an as-of-right development has complied with specific conditions set forth in accordance with provisions of the Zoning Resolution. Certification is also the beginning of the ULURP process indicating that the Department of City Planning has determined that an application is complete and ready for formal public review.

The process by which an owner tells HPD a violation has been fixed, either online through eCertification or on the mailed violation documents. HPD then has 70 days to try to reinspect; the tenant receives a notice of certification in the mail.

An appliance that contains refrigerant (air conditioners, dehumidifiers, refrigerators, freezers, water and wine coolers). DSNY personnel must remove the CFC/Freon by appointment before it is collected with recycling.
Chute: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit), per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Separating or regulating conflicting traffic movements into definite paths using traffic islands or pavement markings, so vehicles and pedestrians move in an orderly way.
The legal document that establishes the organization, powers, functions and procedures of City government, including the sequence of public review for zoning changes.

Pursuant to state law, the City Environmental Quality Review (CEQR) process identifies and assesses the potential environmental impacts of discretionary actions that are proposed by public or private applicants. A discretionary action, such as a zoning map amendment, cannot begin public review until a “conditional negative declaration” or “negative declaration” has been issued, stating that no significant environmental impacts have been identified or, if any potential impacts have been identified, a draft environmental impact statement has been completed, evaluating the significance of identified impacts and proposing appropriate mitigation. A letter “E” designation assigned to a zoning lot indicates a site where environmental requirements must be satisfied before a building permit may be issued for any development, enlargement or change of use.

The City Map is a collection of maps that show legal streets, grades, parks, pierhead and bulkhead lines, public places and other legally established map elements. It is the official map of New York City and is the base for the zoning maps in the Zoning Resolution. The office of each borough president contains the city maps for that borough.

A set of 2023 to 2024 citywide zoning reforms: City of Yes for Carbon Neutrality (energy-efficient buildings and alternative energy infrastructure), City of Yes for Economic Opportunity (modernized use rules allowing a wider range of compatible uses), and City of Yes for Housing Opportunity (more housing types in low-density areas and broader affordable housing programs). DCP calls it the largest change since 1961.

The City Planning Commission, established in 1936, is a 13-member panel responsible for the conduct of planning relating to the orderly growth and development of the city. The Commission meets regularly to hold public hearings and review and vote on applications related to the use and improvement of land, subject to city regulation and a consideration of environmental impacts. The Mayor appoints the Chairperson, who is also Director of the Department of City Planning (DCP), and six other members; each Borough President appoints one member and one member is appointed by the Public Advocate. The DCP provides technical support for the work of the Commission.
A protective or insulating layer fixed to the exterior walls of a building or other structure.
An HPD housing code violation for a non-hazardous condition. The owner has 90 days from notice to correct it before civil penalties begin.
An HPD housing code violation for a hazardous condition. The owner has 30 days from notice to correct it before civil penalties begin.

An HPD housing code violation for an immediately hazardous condition, such as no heat or a lead-based paint hazard to a child. Correction time ranges from immediately (heat and hot water) to 24 hours, 14 days or 21 days depending on the condition. HPD may make the repair itself if the owner does not.
A straight, unobstructed path for pedestrian circulation on the sidewalk (RCNY Title 34, Section 7-06(c)(3)). DCWP's rules and the ADA also define clear path.
A test by a separate, independent certified contractor after lead paint work to confirm no lead dust remains. Required every time work is done in a building covered by Local Law 1.

A detailed, project-specific analysis including a vulnerability and risk assessment, often followed by cost-benefit analysis, used to select investments in climate risk mitigation. Risk is assessed as a function of the likelihood and consequence of a given climate hazard.
Certificate of Occupancy: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Certificate of Correction: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

A request to the Borough Commissioner's office about a plan examiner's objection, or a possible objection on an application not yet filed (pre-determination). File a ZRD1 (zoning) or CCD1 (Construction Code) form, signed and sealed by a professional. Each form is limited to one request and must cite all related Code or Zoning sections.

A value between 0 and 1 measuring how slippery a surface is: the ratio of the resisting force on horizontal motion to the force pressing an object onto the surface. Lower values (like ice) are more slippery; higher values (like concrete) are less slippery.

A street that provides both land access and traffic circulation within residential, commercial and industrial areas, distributing trips from arterials into neighborhoods and channeling traffic from local streets into the arterial system. In the central business district the street grid may serve as the collector system.
Places of business that provide jobs, food and shopping.
A commercial building is any building occupied only by commercial uses, as listed in Use Groups 5 through 16.

A commercial district, designated by the letter C (C1-2, C3, C4-7, for example), is a zoning district in which commercial uses are allowed. Residential and community facility uses may also be permitted.
A C1 or C2 district mapped within a residential zoning district to allow neighborhood-serving retail and related commercial uses on ground floors. Common in areas like Park Slope and Carroll Gardens.
A commercial use is any retail, service or office use listed in Use Groups 5 through 16, or allowed by special permit.

A quality assurance testing process that verifies and documents that selected building systems were designed, installed and work according to the owner's requirements, construction documents and minimum Code. It is mandatory when permitted equipment exceeds a total heating capacity of 600 kBTU/h.
Status for a bill that is sitting with one or more Council committees. While there, members can hold hearings, ask for an analysis of its cost, amend it, and decide whether to vote on it.

A local representative body of 50 members, half nominated by City Council members and half by the Borough President. Boards oversee local government services and advise on land use and liquor license decisions.
A private, federally certified bank or credit union that aims to bring economic equality to underserved communities by lending to small and medium-size businesses.

New York City is organized into 59 community districts. Each CD is represented by a Community Board, composed of volunteer community members appointed by the Borough President, that assist neighborhood residents and advise on neighborhood and citywide planning and service issues.

In the Street Design Manual, streetscape elements that serve street users beyond infrastructure and vehicle operations, such as bike racks, newsstands, public and café seating, public art and plantings. They are generally authorized through permits, revocable consents and/or maintenance agreements. (Different from the zoning meaning.)
A community facility building is any building occupied only by a community facility use(s).
A community facility use provides educational, health, recreational, religious or other essential services for the community it serves. Community facility uses are listed in Use Groups 3 and 4.
The item is tied to a related bill or resolution in a package and cannot advance until that companion item is passed first.

A grant by a City agency for private use of city-owned property in return for compensation beyond an administrative fee. Franchises, revocable consents and leases are not concessions. (NYC Charter Section 362(a))

A SEQR determination that a proposed action would have environmental impacts, but that enforceable conditions imposed on the project can reduce those impacts to a level below significance. Less common than a straight Negative Declaration.

Rules for reading zoning text: words take precedence over drawings or tables; "shall" is mandatory and "may" is permissive; "and" means all listed conditions apply, while "or" means one or more apply.

The former name of the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP): the City agency that licenses and regulates more than 78,000 businesses in 55 industries and enforces the Consumer Protection Law and other City, State and federal laws.

terms.term: Consumer and Worker Protection, NYC Department of
terms.def: The City agency, formerly the Department of Consumer Affairs (DCA), that licenses and regulates more than 78,000 businesses in 55 industries and enforces the Consumer Protection Law and other City, State and federal laws.
DSNY's policy of moving trash out of loose black bags on the street and into bins (NYC Bins for 1 to 9 units, Empire Bins for larger buildings), to reclaim public space and improve quality of life.

Contextual zoning regulates the height and bulk of new buildings, their setback from the street line, and their width along the street frontage, to produce buildings that are consistent with existing neighborhood character. Residential and commercial districts with an A, B, D or X suffix are contextual zoning districts.
Zoning districts developed from the 1980s onward and mapped broadly across the city to preserve existing neighborhood character, prevent out-of-scale development and encourage right-sized growth.

A professional who must be licensed to perform a specific role in getting permits, planning, building, opening or operating a business. Depending on the role, contractors are licensed by DOB (such as general contractors), DCWP (such as home improvement contractors) or another government body.
A conversion is a change of a building’s use to another use.

A protective cap on top of a wall, parapet, pilaster or chimney, often stone, terracotta, concrete, metal or wood. It may be flat, sloped, double-beveled or curved to shed water and protect the masonry below.
The area created by extending the building line to the curb. (Mayor's Executive Order No. 22, April 13, 1995)
Any lot within one hundred feet of the point of intersection of two or more streets. Corner lots have no rear yard requirement and are allowed higher lot coverage.
The corner plus 10 additional feet extending away from the intersection along each intersecting roadway.
A projection that crowns or finishes part of a building, typically the exterior trim where roof meets wall, usually made of bed molding, soffit, fascia and crown molding.

A court is any open area, other than a yard or a portion of a yard, which is unobstructed from its lowest level to the sky, and is bounded by building walls, or building walls and one or more lot lines.
Competent Person: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A collision, as between two automobiles.
A practice at a food establishment that endangers public health and may lower the letter grade from a Health Department inspection. Some must be fixed before food can be served or a permit issued.
When harmful micro-organisms or substances move from one food to another, typically from raw food to ready-to-eat food.
A reference in zoning text to another section, used to point to applicable rules, identify which underlying rule is being modified, or reuse rules without repeating them.

(A) The part of a roadway at an intersection within the extensions of the sidewalk lines on opposite sides, between the curbs or traversable roadway edges; or (B) any part of a roadway, at an intersection or elsewhere, marked for pedestrian crossing by lines or other surface markings. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 110)
Construction Super: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

A discharge of excess wastewater from a combined sewer system (one pipe carrying rainwater runoff, domestic sewage and industrial wastewater) directly into nearby waterways during heavy rain or snowmelt when volume exceeds the capacity of the sewer system or treatment plant.
Cooling Tower: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A concrete border along the roadway that forms the sidewalk edge, which may need a steel face or a row of joined stones.

A curb cut is an angled cut in the edge of a curb that permits vehicular access from a street to a driveway, garage, parking lot or loading dock. In residential districts, width and spacing rules for curb cuts ensure adequate curbside parking.
Rules on the size, number and location of curb cuts accessing parking and loading, ensuring access while limiting effects on sidewalks and on-street parking.

Curb level is the mean level of the curb adjoining a zoning lot. In general, it is the basis for building height and setback controls in medium- and higher- density non-contextual districts and manufacturing districts.
The line along the face of the street curb next to the roadway.
DSNY's weekly collection of leaf and yard waste, food scraps, food-soiled paper and certified compostable products, picked up on your recycling day. Mandatory citywide since April 1, 2025.
The outer skin of a building: a non-load-bearing wall of glass, metal or masonry attached to the building's structural frame.
Traffic using minor roadways, usually residential streets, as shortcuts to avoid congestion on major streets.
Design Drawings: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Department of Design & Construction: an abbreviation for a government agency, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

terms.term: DEC (New York State Department of Environmental Conservation)
terms.def: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation: an abbreviation for a government agency, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
The bill came to a vote and failed because more members voted against it than for it.
Action on the item has been put off to a later date. This is often seen with land use items that still need negotiation before a vote.

Words given a specific meaning in the Zoning Resolution, shown in orange italics on the Online ZR. Core definitions are in Section 12-10; chapters may add their own. Common words can have special zoning meanings; "building" has a 200+ word definition.
Demolition: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Work that takes apart or tears down a structure, including part of an interior during a business remodel. DOB requires a work permit.

Density refers to the maximum number of dwelling units permitted on a zoning lot. The factors for each district are approximations of average unit size plus allowances for any common areas. Special density regulations apply to mixed buildings that contain both residential and community facility uses.

terms.term: DEP (New York City Department of Environmental Protection)
terms.def: New York City Department of Environmental Protection: an abbreviation for a government agency, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
The City agency that applicants work with to prepare land use applications, that publishes the Zoning Handbook and Online ZR, and that runs the Zoning Help Desk (212-720-3291).

terms.term: Department of Consumer Affairs Adjudication Tribunal
terms.def: An administrative court that hears cases on violations of the City's licensing laws, the Consumer Protection Law and other laws enforced by DCWP.
The life expectancy of an asset or product as determined during design.

A selected speed used to determine a roadway's geometric design features. It should be logical given topography, anticipated operating speed, adjacent land use and the road's functional classification.
A selected vehicle, with representative weight, dimensions and operating characteristics, used to set roadway design controls for accommodating vehicles of designated classes.

A zoning designation on a property for hazardous materials, noise or air quality so mitigation requirements are easy to find. The Office of Environmental Remediation (OER) must confirm required mitigations before DOB issues construction permits. Sites are listed in a Zoning Resolution appendix and on ZoLa.

A development includes the construction of a new building or other structure on a zoning lot, the relocation of an existing building to another zoning lot, or the establishment of a new open use on a tract of land.
An online hub that speeds approval of construction projects by letting architects and engineers submit digital construction plans to City agencies.

Development rights generally refer to the maximum amount of floor area permissible on a zoning lot. When the actual built floor area is less than the maximum permitted floor area, the difference is referred to as “unused development rights.” Unused development rights are often described as air rights. A zoning lot merger is the joining of two or more adjacent zoning lots into one new zoning lot. Unused development rights may be shifted from one lot to another, as-of-right, only through a zoning lot merger. A transfer of development rights (TDR) allows for the transfer of unused development rights from one zoning lot to another in limited circumstances, usually to promote the preservation of historic buildings, open space or unique cultural resources. For such purposes, a TDR may be permitted where the transfer could not be accomplished through a zoning lot merger. In the case of a landmark building, for example, a transfer may be made by CPC special permit from the zoning lot containing the designated landmark to an adjacent zoning lot or one that is directly across a street or, for a corner lot, another corner lot on the same intersection.
Wages that make up for lost pay due to permanent physical or mental impairment, as required by federal law.

A program that freezes the rent of eligible tenants 18 or older who receive SSI, SSDI, or certain VA, Postal Service or Medicaid disability benefits. Household income must be $50,000 or less, rent must exceed one-third of income, and the apartment must be regulated by HCR.
The status of an application that is not approved at a given moment. Applications can usually be changed and resubmitted for approval without starting over.

An action that requires a government agency to make a judgment-based decision, as opposed to ministerial or as-of-right approvals. Discretionary actions typically require ULURP, SEQR/CEQR review, or both. CB6 reviews discretionary actions within its boundaries.
District: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Required separation, ranging from 10 to 80 feet, when a single lot includes more than one building and one contains residences. The required distance increases with density and building height.
A sidewalk with different material, color, scoring and/or dimensions than DOT's standard sidewalk. Distinctive sidewalks require Public Design Commission (PDC) approval.

A letter or number appended to a zoning district name (for example the "-2" in M1-2 or the "A" in R3A). Suffixes generally reflect subtle variations in permitted building scale; an M1-2 district typically allows one or two more stories than an M1-1. A rule listing "R3" applies to all R3 variations, while one listing only "R3-2" applies just to that variation.

An HPD division that surveys buildings in poor overall condition and works with owners and tenants to stabilize them. It also gives owners free one-on-one counseling on Housing Maintenance Code requirements, removing violations, and available loans, grants and tax benefits.
Door Lock Monitoring: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Demolition and Removal: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit), per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Department of Buildings: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
The Department of Buildings' online portal for filing applications and permits.
A Department of Buildings office that tenants affected by construction in occupied multiple dwellings can contact at (212) 393-2949 or TenantAdvocate@buildings.nyc.gov.
Document: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

A docket is the Department of City Planning's official description of a proposed land-use action. The docket description is incorporated in the Commission's and City Council's resolution of approval and, except for City Map actions, is the legal and binding description of the action.

terms.term: DOH (New York State Department of Health)
terms.def: New York State Department of Health: an abbreviation for a government agency, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
The name customers see for a business, which may differ from its name on legal documents. See also Certificate of Assumed Name.

A dormer is a permitted obstruction within a required setback area that may exceed the height of a building. In lower-density districts, it is often a window protruding from a sloped roof to provide light and air to the top floors of homes. In R6 through R10 contextual districts, dormers are portions of buildings allowed to penetrate a required setback above the maximum base height in order to provide variety to the base heights of buildings along a street. Both types of dormers are subject to size limitations.

terms.term: DOT (New York City Department of Transportation)
terms.def: New York City Department of Transportation: an abbreviation for a government agency, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

A lock that requires a key from inside the apartment to unlock a door, or a window gate that needs a key to reach the hallway or fire escape. Both are dangerous and illegal and must be removed. Legal window gates open with a latch and carry an NYC approval label.

Storm water on the sidewalk and roadway along a property must drain into a street drainage system. Storm water falling on-site, as DEP allows, goes to an on-site drywell or similar, or connects to the storm water system or Green Infrastructure at the street.
Every person who operates, drives or is in actual physical control of a vehicle. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 113)
Every entrance or exit authorized under applicable law and used by vehicles to or from lands or buildings abutting a highway. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))
Any building or structure, or part of one, occupied in whole or in part as the home, residence or sleeping place of one or more people.

A dwelling unit consists of one or more rooms that contain lawful cooking and sanitary facilities, inhabited by one or more persons living together and maintaining a common household, in a residential building or residential portion of a building.

The number used to cap the number of apartments on a zoning lot. In most areas, the maximum is permitted residential floor area divided by 680 square feet (20,000 square feet allows 29 units). It sets a minimum average unit size, not a minimum size per unit. Some housing, such as in the Manhattan Core and Downtown Brooklyn, is exempt.

Covered electronic equipment under the NYS Electronic Equipment Recycling and Reuse Act, such as computers, monitors, TVs, printers, phones, tablets, game consoles and their cords. Illegal to put out with trash or recycling.
Earthwork: a DOB permit type code, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
An e-waste recycling option residents can use through enrollment of apartment buildings with 10 or more units.
Effective: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Raising a building so its lowest occupied floor is above flood levels shown on FEMA flood maps, as described in Building Code Appendix G and Zoning Resolution Article VI, Chapter 4.

The HPD program that fixes immediately hazardous (Class C) conditions when the owner does not. HPD hires a contractor and bills the owner through the Department of Finance for the cost plus fees; unpaid bills become a tax lien on the property that bears interest.

A sealed, stationary on-street trash container assigned to a larger apartment building or school, opened with a key card and emptied by DSNY's automated side-loading trucks. In use in M9 and BK2, with a citywide goal by 2032.
A tax form employees give their employer so the correct federal income tax is withheld from their pay.
A number used to identify and track a business for federal tax purposes, also called a Federal Tax Identification Number.
A form employers must complete for each new hire to prove the person is legally allowed to work in the United States.
The Council has passed the local law and it is awaiting the Mayor. Under the City Charter the Mayor has 30 days to sign it, veto it, or take no action, in which case it becomes law anyway.
Parts of a building that intrude onto a sidewalk and/or street, including vaults, steps, stoops, footings, fences and retaining walls.

Created in 2023, a defined term grouping renewable energy generation (such as solar panels) and energy storage (such as batteries) into a single use, allowed in all districts subject to size and screening rules. See ZR Section 12-10.
A soil designed to achieve specific infiltration standards in a stormwater-capture installation.

HPD programs for buildings that fail to fix conditions or let violations pile up. They can lead to emergency repair charges, fees, relocation liens and civil penalties billed to the property, and in the most serious cases a court-appointed administrator who controls the building day to day.
An enlargement is a built addition to an existing building that increases the floor area of the building.

A standardized form used under SEQR/CEQR to assess whether a proposed action may have significant environmental impacts. Applicants complete Part 1; the lead agency completes Parts 2 and 3. The EAF determines whether a full Environmental Impact Statement is required.
A City court that handles quality-of-life violations, such as sanitation and noise, in New York City.
A non-criminal quality-of-life violation, such as a dirty sidewalk or lack of rodent control, issued by several City agencies and heard by the Environmental Control Board.

A detailed study of a proposed action's potential environmental impacts, required when a lead agency issues a Positive Declaration under SEQR/CEQR. Includes a draft EIS (public comment period), scoping, and final EIS. CB6 can participate in scoping and comment on the draft.
The City agency charged with protecting New York City's natural environment.
Review required for zoning changes and other discretionary actions to consider a project's potential environmental impacts and ways to address them.
Construction Equipment: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit), per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Equipment Work: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit), per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

Moving earth, rock or other material with tools, equipment or explosives, including earthwork, trenching, wall shafts and tunneling. Under BC 3302.1 it is removing earth from its natural position, except incidental removal during augering, drilling, vibrating or driving. Coordination with FDNY is required.
Exposure: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Exterior: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
An extension is an expansion of the existing floor area occupied by an existing use.
Fire Alarm: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit), per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
The exterior wall of a building, often used to install antennas.

A joint effort of HPD and the NYC Commission on Human Rights that explains protected classes, who can be liable for discrimination, how to file a complaint, and affordable housing opportunities (nyc.gov/fairhousing).

Districts often set different maximum FARs for residential, commercial and community facility uses. These are not added together: the highest maximum FAR among uses on the lot sets the overall limit, and each use must stay within its own maximum.
Fuel Burning: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit), per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Federal Emergency Management Agency: an abbreviation for a government agency, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

In residential districts, the maximum height of a fence constructed along a front lot line is four feet above ground level. The maximum height of a fence along the side or rear lot line is six feet. In most instances, fences are considered permitted obstructions.
The bill is no longer active. This happens when a committee recommends it be filed (dropped) or when its sponsor leaves the Council.
A hired third party who, for a fee, carries documents between an architect, engineer or contractor and City agencies.

terms.term: Financial Services, New York State Department of
terms.def: The State agency that regulates state-licensed and state-chartered financial institutions, and helps people and businesses understand financial products and make insurance and other claims.

Specific criteria that an agency must affirmatively determine before granting a discretionary approval. For example, all five BSA variance findings under ZR §72-21 must be met. If required findings cannot be made, approval must be denied.

The City agency responsible for fire safety citywide. It oversees fire risk and public safety rules, reviews construction plans and inspects businesses for issues like kitchens, exits and large gathering spaces.

A person holding a certificate of fitness who keeps a fire watch. DOB or HPD may order an owner to provide one when construction leaves egress blocked, fire-rated material missing, or fire protection not working; they generally cost about $750 to $1,250 per 24 hours.
An FDNY-required notice owners must post on the inside of every apartment door and in common areas and distribute to each unit, to new tenants, and annually during fire prevention week.
Building parts made of non-combustible materials with fire-resistance ratings at least equal to those required for the same parts of a fireproof dwelling.
A flat slab of stone used as a paving material.

The envelope for districts that allow rowhouses and apartment buildings with flat roofs. Maximum heights range from 35 to hundreds of feet depending on district. Districts with letter suffixes typically require all buildings to follow flat roof envelopes.
A fixed vertical structure designed to prevent flooding from an adjacent river or waterway.

The floor area of a building is the sum of the gross area of each floor of the building, excluding mechanical space, cellar space, floor space in open balconies, elevators or stair bulkheads and, in most zoning districts, floor space used for accessory parking that is located less than 23 feet above curb level.

Extra floor area granted in exchange for providing a public amenity, such as a public plaza, visual or performing arts space, subway improvements, theater preservation or a grocery store. Some bonuses are as-of-right; others need CPC and City Council approval.

The primary zoning control for building size: total building floor area divided by the area of the zoning lot. A FAR of 2.0 on a 5,000 sq ft lot allows up to 10,000 sq ft of floor area. Higher FAR = larger buildings permitted.
An official drawing by a licensed professional of an existing or planned space seen from above, with technical details; sometimes called blueprints. See also Site Plans.
Fence: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit), per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Foundation: a DOB permit type code, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

A certificate earned by completing the Health Department's course on safely preparing and serving food. A worker holding one must be present at all times while food is prepared or served at a food service establishment.
All food waste, including meat, bones, shells, dairy and prepared or cooked food. Must be separated from trash for composting.
A place that serves food directly to customers, such as a restaurant, bakery, coffee shop or bar.
Paper contaminated with food, such as greasy, uncoated paper plates and pizza boxes. Goes in compost, not recycling.

The base of a building, typically concrete with wood or steel structural elements driven into the ground or cast in place. It may be a mat foundation, a slab-on-grade, or individual or strip footings.
Fire Suppression: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit), per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A dwelling whose exterior walls, or any structural parts of them, are made of wood.

A grant by a City agency of a right to occupy or use the city's inalienable property (usually streets or sidewalks) to provide a public service. (NYC Charter Section 362(b)) Example: the Coordinated Street Furniture Franchise for bus shelters, newsstands, public toilets and bike shelters.
A FRESH food store is a full-line grocery store, established in underserved neighborhoods through zoning incentives, that promotes the sale of fresh food products.
A front yard line is a line drawn parallel to the front lot line at the depth of a required front yard.
Fuel Storage: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit), per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Full Stop Work Order: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Failure to Comply: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Failure to Maintain: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

The section of sidewalk between the curb and the through (walking) zone where street furniture and amenities go, such as lighting, benches, wayfinding signs, utility poles, tree pits and bike parking. It may include green infrastructure like rain gardens. The Manual treats the street furniture/curb zone as the same thing.
A combination of traffic calming and visual measures at the entrance to a low-speed street to slow entering vehicles and discourage through-traffic.
General Contractor: a DOB abbreviation for a construction professional and an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
The Council's list of items cleared by committee and waiting for a vote of the full Council. A bill placed here needs no further committee action.
A practice at a food establishment that poses risks to public health and may lower the letter grade from a Health Department inspection.
Ground Fault Circuit Interrupter: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

This glossary provides brief explanations of planning and zoning terminology, including terms highlighted in the Zoning Handbook. Words and phrases followed by an asterisk (*) in the Glossary are legally defined terms in the Zoning Resolution of the City of New York, and can be found primarily in Section 12-10 of the Resolution for the complete legal definitions.
A system that separates fats, oils and grease from wastewater to prevent sewer clogs. DEP requires them for food service establishments and some other businesses.

The combined transit-oriented parking area that the handbook's charts divide into the Inner Transit Zone and Outer Transit Zone. Outside it ("beyond the Greater Transit Zone"), parking is required for most residential and non-residential developments.

Products, technologies and practices that use natural systems, or engineered systems that mimic them, to improve environmental quality and provide utility services. Typically soils and vegetation infiltrate, evapotranspire and/or detain stormwater; they can also filter air, reduce energy use, cool urban heat islands and store carbon.

A vegetated area and its pathways within the right-of-way under DOT jurisdiction and maintained by Parks under an agreement between the two agencies. Greenstreets do not include Stormwater Greenstreets.
A group parking facility is a building, structure or lot used for parking that serves more than one dwelling unit.
The part of the street extending 18 inches from the curb. Property owners must keep it clean along with the sidewalk.
A sink used only for washing hands, required in every bathroom and within 25 clear feet of anywhere a worker prepares or serves food. See also Ware Washing Sinks.
Making infrastructure less susceptible to damage from external security, safety and climate threats, such as extreme wind, flooding or flying debris.

A finding that the cost of LPC-compliant preservation would make a property economically undevelopable. An owner can apply for a hardship determination from LPC, which may allow modifications to otherwise required preservation standards.

terms.term: Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point Plan
terms.def: A document that tracks food from arrival at an establishment until it is served, identifying food safety threats and ways to eliminate them. See also Potentially Hazardous Food.

terms.term: Health and Mental Hygiene, NYC Department of
terms.def: The City agency that oversees health and safety rules in New York City, including inspecting food service establishments and licensing various businesses.
Risk management that protects one or more people against health care costs. Most employees in New York can get it through their employers. See also Insurance.
Means a Council committee has held a public hearing on the bill, where residents, city agencies, advocates and experts could give testimony for or against it.
The period from October 1 to May 31 when building owners must provide heat to apartments.

An HPD program that selects 50 buildings each year with a history of heat violations and requires owners to install internet-capable heat sensors in every unit. HPD inspects these buildings during heat season without waiting for complaints.

Rules that shape the volume of a building above its footprint, defining the "envelope" its permitted floor area must fit within, so new buildings do not overwhelm their surroundings while still allowing design flexibility.

The height factor of a building is equal to the total floor area of the building divided by its lot coverage (in square feet). In general, the height factor is equal to the number of stories in a building constructed without setbacks.

A height factor building is a building containing residences whose residential bulk is determined by a complementary range of height factors, floor area ratios and open space ratios, and is set within a sky exposure plane. Height factor regulations promote tall buildings surrounded by open space. Height factor buildings are permitted only in R6 through R9 non-contextual districts.

Group H occupancy covers using a building, or part of one, to manufacture, process, generate or store materials that are a physical or health hazard in excess quantities (BC Tables 307(1) and 307(2)). Zoning Use Group 18 addresses hazardous materials.

The highest level of groundwater in an area, accounting for seasonal and storm-driven fluctuations. It varies across the boroughs and must be considered when designing stormwater management or green infrastructure.
The entire width between the boundary lines of every publicly maintained way when any part is open to the public for vehicle travel. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 118)

A defined area designated by the LPC for its architectural, cultural, or historic significance. Exterior changes to buildings within a historic district generally require a Certificate of Appropriateness from LPC. In CB6, major historic districts include Park Slope, Cobble Hill, Carroll Gardens, and Boerum Hill.
Hoist Machine Operator: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
The temperature at which certain foods must be kept before cooking or serving, monitored according to Health Department guidelines. See also Potentially Hazardous Food.

A Housing Court case to evict a tenant for reasons other than unpaid rent, such as a lease breach, nuisance, illegal sublet, non-primary residence, illegal use, or lease expiration where no renewal is required by law. The owner must first serve a notice ending the lease.

A home occupation is a business operated by the occupant(s) of a dwelling unit, which is accessory to the residential use. It is generally restricted to no more than 25 percent of the floor area of the dwelling unit (500 sq ft maximum). Occupations that may generate excessive noise, odors or pedestrian traffic are not permitted.
A home repair loan program for homeowners that the Homeowner Help Desk helps people access.

An HPD and CNYCN service giving homeowners at risk of displacement one-on-one housing, financial and legal counseling, help spotting deed theft and scams, and help applying to programs such as PTAID and HomeFix (1-855-HOME-456).
Sideways movement of vehicles forced by physical and/or visual changes to roadway alignment, such as a bend in the road. A traffic calming technique.
The number in a street address identifying residential and commercial buildings, used in DOB's Building Information System and the same as the one the US Postal Service uses.
An HPD network of community organizations that help people prepare and apply for affordable housing lotteries.

NYC's official platform for affordable housing lottery applications. Residents can apply for income-restricted units across the city. CB6's Rental Rankings & Housing tab includes direct links to active lotteries.
The court where tenants in privately owned buildings can sue an owner over repairs or harassment (an HP Action), and the only place an owner can legally evict a tenant.
A hotline (212-962-4795, 9am to 5pm Monday through Thursday) that explains Housing Court procedures and landlord-tenant rules and refers people to free legal help and community organizations.
The HPD division that may take legal action against an owner when a reinspection finds that a violation certified as corrected was not fixed.
The City law that sets the standards owners must meet so that apartments and common areas are safe and well maintained. HPD enforces it by inspecting buildings and issuing violations.

A case a tenant brings in Housing Court against an owner for repair problems or harassment. The tenant can request an inspection before the court date; an HPD attorney is present, and the judge may order the owner to fix violations by a deadline and may impose civil penalties or contempt if the owner does not.
Housing Preservation and Development: an abbreviation for a government agency, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

The yearly registration owners file with HPD for buildings with three or more units, and 1-2 family homes where neither the owner nor immediate family lives. HPD uses it to contact owners about complaints and violations, and other agencies use it in emergencies.

The HPD division that inspects buildings in response to complaints and issues violations of the Housing Maintenance Code. Inspectors also check safety items such as smoke detectors. Brooklyn offices are at 345 Adams Street (212-863-8060) and 701 Euclid Avenue (212-863-6620).

The HPD office that runs financing programs offering low-interest loans and property tax exemptions to keep privately owned multifamily and owner-occupied buildings physically and financially sound and affordable.
HPD's website where anyone can check the status of a 311 complaint, see whether an inspection was done, and view all open violations on a building.
Homeowner Resolution Program: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Interim Certificate of Occupancy: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

terms.term: IESNA (Illuminating Engineering Society of North America)
terms.def: A professional organization of lighting engineers that has set recommended illumination levels for street and pedestrian lighting.
A sign plugged into electricity, such as a neon "Open" sign. DOB regulates these separately from other signs. See also Sign.

terms.term: Imminent Health Hazard (or Public Health Hazard) in Food Safety
terms.def: A practice at a food establishment that immediately threatens public health. If found during a Health Department inspection, it must be corrected before the restaurant can reopen or receive a grade.

Incentive zoning provides a bonus, usually in the form of additional floor area, in exchange for the provision of a public amenity or affordable housing. There are incentive bonuses for the provision of public plazas (privately owned public spaces), visual or performing arts spaces, subway improvements, theater preservation, FRESH food stores and affordable housing (Inclusionary Housing Program).
An online tool that helps new or existing businesses find City, State and federal financial incentives they may be eligible for.

The Inclusionary Housing Program provides two optional floor area incentives in exchange for the creation or preservation of affordable housing, on or off-site, predominantly for low-income households. The original R10 Program provides a floor area bonus of up to 20 percent, increasing the maximum FAR of 10.0 to 12.0 for the provision of affordable housing in applicable residential and commercial districts with R10 density. In Inclusionary Housing designated areas* mapped in medium- and high- density residential neighborhoods and commercial districts with equivalent density, a bonus of 33 percent of floor area can be obtained for providing 20 percent as affordable housing. The base FAR in designated areas is, in most cases, lower than the maximum FAR allowed in the same zoning district located outside a designated area.
The process of creating convenient, safe and accessible spaces for everyone, with accessibility a critical component. The Manual uses "inclusive design" instead of "universal design."

A dwelling unit that complies with the definition of an affordable housing unit under one of the Inclusionary Housing Programs, or any other dwelling unit with a legally binding restriction on household income at or below 80 percent of Area Median Income.
A drain pipe that does not connect directly to a drain but empties through an air gap into a drain or other plumbing, so waste below the gap cannot back up into the pipe above.

An improvement to an individual rent-regulated apartment that can be a basis for a rent increase. Tenants can contact HCR about IAI rent increases or seek legal counsel on whether an increase is legal.
Places where things are made, from factories to workshops, where ideas take physical shape.
A parking area where zoning does not require parking for residential developments and often not for non-residential developments.
Inspection: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
The set period, such as once a year, within which many businesses, buildings and license holders are checked for compliance. Cycles can vary, sometimes based on past inspection results.

Financial protection against loss: you pay a set amount each period and are paid for losses from unplanned events. Many types are required to own or lease space or employ workers, and proof of insurance is required for certain permits and licenses.

A Loft Building meeting the criteria in MDL Section 281, as decided by the Loft Board. Under MDL 280, IMDs are treated as lawfully existing multiple dwellings even if legalization (the process to reach compliance and get a Certificate of Occupancy) has not started.
Any zoning lot that is neither a corner lot nor a through lot.
The federal agency that collects taxes from individuals and businesses.
The area within the grid created by extending the curblines of two or more streets where they cross. (RCNY Title 34, Section 2-01)
The first official step for a City Council bill: a member files it, it gets an Intro number, and the Speaker refers it to a committee to study it.
The broad category of work in a DOB permit application, such as NB for New Building and Alt-1, Alt-2 and Alt-3 for alteration types.
Joint living-work quarters for artists are spaces in nonresidential buildings used for living quarters and work space by artists and their households.
Job Schedule of Occupancy: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
The court judgment and warrant an owner must obtain, directing a City marshal to carry out an eviction.
Limited Alteration Application: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

terms.term: Labor, New York State Department of
terms.def: The State agency that oversees laws on worker safety and fair labor practices.
The federal agency that oversees laws on workers' rights, safety, health and income stability.
The committee took up the bill (often at a hearing) but chose not to vote yet. The bill remains pending in that committee and can come back at a later meeting.

The application, prepared with the Department of City Planning, to change zoning or obtain another land use approval. It includes any required environmental review. Once DCP certifies it as complete, it goes before the City Planning Commission and public review begins.
A building or site legally recognized for its historic value, regulated by the Landmarks Preservation Commission and requiring special permission to change.

The city agency responsible for designating and regulating landmarks and historic districts in New York City. LPC designates individual landmarks, interior landmarks, scenic landmarks, and historic districts. CB6 has 6 historic districts within its boundaries.
The legal approval of a space's owner for a business's use of that space.
Anything too large to fit into a bin or bag. NYC residents get free curbside removal, up to 6 items per collection day.

A large-scale development is a development generally involving several zoning lots planned as a unit. Large-scale development regulations allow modifications to various zoning regulations, such as the distribution of floor area without regard to zoning lot lines, by CPC discretionary action. Such modifications can allow for design flexibility to achieve a superior site plan. A large-scale general development* is a development or enlargement for any uses permitted by the underlying district regulations in commercial districts (except C1, C2, C3 and C4-1 districts) and in all manufacturing districts. The development must be on a tract of land that is at least 1.5 acres and may include existing buildings. A large-scale residential development* is a development designed predominantly for residential uses in residence districts and in C1, C2, C3 and C4-1 districts. The development must be on a tract of land that is either at least three acres (130,680 sq ft) with a minimum of 500 dwelling units or at least 1.5 acres (65,340 sq ft) with a minimum of three principal residential buildings. Existing buildings may not form any part of a large-scale residential development. A large-scale community facility development * is a development or enlargement predominantly for community facility uses in residential districts and in C1, C2, C3 and C4-1 districts. The development must be on a tract of land that is at least three acres (130,680 sq ft) and may include existing buildings.
Changes to a floor layout that add, move, remodel, enlarge or shrink interior rooms while keeping the same building envelope.
Lift Director: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

The government agency designated to coordinate the SEQR/CEQR environmental review when multiple agencies have approval authority over an action. The lead agency conducts the EAF review, makes the significance determination, and, if required, oversees the EIS process.

An HPD exemption an owner can apply for after showing an apartment has no lead-based paint or after abating it with certified workers. Once granted, the lease and annual inquiry, visual inspection, and certified-contractor requirements no longer apply.

Deteriorated lead paint, dust or chips that young children can swallow, causing behavioral and learning problems. Under Local Law 1, a hazard is presumed in a building built before 1960 with three or more apartments (or a rented unit in a 1-2 family home) where a child under six lives or spends 10 or more hours a week.
