Leaves, flowers, houseplants, twigs, branches, grass clippings and Christmas trees. Must be separated from trash and set out for composting.
A legal agreement between an owner (lessor) and a user (lessee) of a space, which helps define what activities are allowed there.

A light source that converts electricity to light through the movement of electrons, with no filament. It is more efficient than incandescent bulbs, uses less energy, is more compact and lasts longer.
A grade card issued by the Health Department summarizing a restaurant's inspection results for customers. It must be displayed at all food service establishments; "A" is the highest grade.

terms.term: Letter of No Objection (for units under the Loft Law)
terms.def: A letter (LNO) the owner must get from the Loft Board before obtaining a permit for other work in the building that is not directly related to the IMD unit(s).
The legal responsibility of a party to repay debts it made, or that another party legally tied to it made. For example, a business partner may be liable to the business.
License: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

Older term, replaced by Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation in the 2008 NYC Building Code. Under the 1938 Code it identified assembly spaces whose lawful use depended on a license from the Fire Department, Police Department or Department of Licenses.
A licensed private hauler that businesses must hire to collect their recycling.

A limited height district may be superimposed on an area designated as an historic district by the Landmarks Preservation Commission. It is mapped in areas of the Upper East Side, Gramercy Park, Brooklyn Heights and Cobble Hill. The maximum building height is 50 feet in a LH-1 district, 60 feet in a LH- 1A district, 70 feet in a LH-2 district and 100 feet in a LH-3 district.
A legally mapped street temporarily closed to motor vehicles by DOT, in accordance with authorized signs or other traffic control devices. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-12(r)(4))
A horizontal structural member, such as a beam, over a door or window opening that carries the wall above. Usually steel, precast concrete, stone or wood.
Permission from the State Liquor Authority for a business to serve alcohol. Different licenses apply to different business types, types of alcohol, and on-site or off-site consumption.
Local Law: an abbreviation DOB uses for a law, code or policy document, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Letter of No Objection: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

An off-street space where trucks pick up or deliver goods, required for new buildings with commercial or manufacturing uses. The number depends on use, size and district; uses are grouped into five Loading Requirement Categories. Loading areas are exempt from floor area up to 150 percent of the required amount.

terms.term: Local Law 1 of 2004 (Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention Act)
terms.def: NYC's lead paint law. It requires owners of covered pre-1960 buildings (and 1960 to 1978 buildings known to have lead paint) to ask about young children, inspect yearly, fix hazards with certified workers and safe work practices, do turnover work, test units by XRF, and keep records. Since February 2021 it applies to 1-2 unit homes with tenants.

The City law on indoor allergen hazards such as mold and pests. Owners must give each tenant, with the lease, a fact sheet and notice explaining the owner's duty to keep the building free of indoor allergens.

Part of the Climate Mobilization Act of 2019, it sets increasingly strict greenhouse gas emissions caps on the city's largest buildings, most over 25,000 square feet, starting in 2024. Buildings over their limits face financial penalties; affordable and rent-regulated buildings are covered but treated differently.
A street not on the higher (collector or arterial) systems. It mainly provides direct access to abutting land and to higher-order streets; through-traffic is usually discouraged.
Vehicle traffic whose trip origin and/or destination is in the immediate area of a given street.

A loft is a building or space within a building designed for commercial or manufacturing use, generally constructed prior to 1930. In certain manufacturing districts, lofts may be converted to residential use by CPC special permit.

The New York City Loft Board, a nine-member board appointed by the Mayor, created by the State Legislature in 1982 to regulate converting certain commercial and manufacturing buildings to lawful residential use.

Before a permit for work to legalize IMD unit(s), once owner and occupants resolve all objections and issues, the Loft Board issues a letter certifying compliance with all Loft Board requirements and stating it has no objections.

A method of measuring traffic flow based on delay and congestion, defined in the Highway Capacity Manual, graded A (free flow) to F (traffic jam). Historically used mainly for motor vehicles, LOS methods also exist for pedestrians, cyclists and transit.
Lot area is the area (in square feet) of a zoning lot.
Lot coverage is that portion of a zoning lot which, when viewed from above, is covered by a building. Permitted obstructions are not counted towards lot coverage calculations.
Lot depth is the mean horizontal distance between the front lot line and rear lot line of a zoning lot.

terms.term: Lot Line or Zoning Lot Line
terms.def: A lot line or a zoning lot line is a boundary of a zoning lot. A front lot line,* also known as a street line, is that portion of a zoning lot line that fronts upon a street. A rear lot line* is any lot line that is generally parallel to a street line bounding the zoning lot and does not intersect a street line. A side lot line* is any lot line that is neither a front lot line nor a rear lot line.

Windows in an exterior wall on a side or rear zoning or tax lot line. They require special Code review, based on building type and construction class, to set allowable window size, number and fire protection.

A lot or zoning lot is a tract of land comprising a single tax lot or two or more adjacent tax lots within a block. An apartment building on a single zoning lot, for example, may contain separate condominium units, each occupying its own tax lot. Similarly, a building containing a row of townhouses may occupy several separate tax lots within a single zoning lot, or two or more detached homes on one zoning lot may each have its own tax lot. The zoning lot is the basic unit for zoning regulations and may be subdivided into two or more zoning lots, and two or more adjoining zoning lots on the same block may be merged, provided that all resulting zoning lots comply with applicable regulations. A corner lot* is a zoning lot that adjoins the point of intersection of two or more streets; it is also a zoning lot bounded entirely by streets. An interior lot* is any zoning lot that is neither a corner lot nor a through lot. A through lot* is any zoning lot that connects two generally parallel streets and is not a corner lot.
Lot width is the mean horizontal distance between the side lot lines of a zoning lot.

A Lower Density Growth Management Area is a designated area that is generally distant from mass transit and characterized by rapid growth and high auto ownership, such as Staten Island or the Throgs Neck area of the Bronx. New developments must provide more off-street parking, larger yards and more open space than would otherwise be required in the mapped zoning districts.

terms.term: LPC (New York City Landmark Preservation Commission)
terms.def: New York City Landmark Preservation Commission: an abbreviation for a government agency, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Legal Policy and Procedures Notice: an abbreviation DOB uses for a law, code or policy document, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

Created in 2024, a framework of 15 new Manufacturing Districts ranging from 2 to 15 FAR that mimic older loft building forms and come in several use-mix options. First applied in the Atlantic Avenue Mixed Use area in Brooklyn. See Article IV.

An existing building 10 or more stories or 125 feet or more tall, or with a footprint of 100,000 square feet or more regardless of height, or one the Commissioner designates because of unique construction or demolition hazards.

A building-wide improvement in a rent-regulated building that can be a basis for a rent increase. Tenants can contact HCR about MCI rent increases or seek legal counsel on whether an increase is legal.

A city program, adopted in 2016, that requires a percentage of units in newly-rezoned areas to be permanently affordable. Several options exist, including 25% of units at 60% AMI or 30% at 80% AMI. MIH applies to all rezonings that allow residential use.

The Manhattan Core extends from the southern tip of Manhattan at The Battery to West 110th Street on the West Side and East 96th Street on the East Side. It is the area covered by Manhattan Community Districts 1 through 8.

terms.term: Manhattan Core and Long Island City (parking areas)
terms.def: Areas where zoning requires no parking for any use. The Manhattan Core is Community Districts 1 to 8; it has strict limits on permitted parking and does not allow off-site parking. Their parking rules are in Article I, Chapters 3 and 6.

A manufacturing district, designated by the letter M (M1-1, M2-2, for example), is a zoning district in which manufacturing uses, most commercial uses and some community facility uses are permitted. Industrial uses are subject to a range of performance standards. Residential development is not allowed, except in M1-1D through M1-5D districts by CPC authorization, and in M1-6D districts, as-of-right or by CPC certification.
A manufacturing use is any use listed in Use Group 17 or 18, or an industrial use only allowed by special permit.
A City office that publishes information on tenant protection laws, including rent regulation (nyc.gov/tenantprotection).
Multiple Dwelling Law: an abbreviation DOB uses for a law, code or policy document and an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Mechanical: a DOB permit type code, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Mechanical/HVAC: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit), per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Small vehicles such as scooters and bikes that people use for quick trips.

Minimum lot area and lot width rules governing how a larger lot can be divided, most impactful for single- and two-family houses in lower-density areas. The largest minimums apply in the lowest-density districts.
The least an employee must be paid per hour of work, set by City, State and federal law. See also Wages.
Miscellaneous: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A measure identified in environmental review to address a project's potential environmental impacts.

A mixed building is a building in a commercial district used partly for residential use and partly for community facility or commercial use. When a building contains more than one use, the maximum FAR permitted on the zoning lot is the highest FAR allowed for any of the uses, provided that the FAR for each use does not exceed the maximum FAR permitted for that use. In a C1-8A district, for example, where the maximum commercial FAR is 2.0 and the maximum residential FAR is 7.52, the total permitted FAR for a mixed residential/commercial building would be 7.52, of which no more than 2.0 FAR may be applied to the commercial space.
Under the Building Code, a building containing two or more occupancy classifications, which may or may not match the zoning use groups. The DOB glossary gives the same definition for Mixed Use.
Newspapers, magazines, office and colored paper, envelopes, paperback books and similar paper, recycled together with cardboard in a labeled bin or clear bag.
Combining shops, homes and offices in the same building.

A mixed use district is a special purpose district where one set of regulations applies to many different areas shown on the zoning maps as MX with a numerical suffix (MX-8, for example). In MX districts, an M1 district is paired with a residential district (M1-2/R6, for example) and new residential and non- residential uses are permitted as-of-right within the same building. In this district, a building that contains a residential use and any other use is a mixed use building.

A single pole that supports an antenna or sign, typically 50 to 120 feet tall but variable. Code requires it be bolted to or embedded in a concrete foundation sized to resist the loads on the structure.

terms.term: MOPD (Mayor Office for People with Disabilities)
terms.def: Mayor Office for People with Disabilities: an abbreviation for a government agency, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

Every vehicle operated or driven on a public highway that is propelled by any power other than muscular power, except as provided in Section 125 of the Vehicle and Traffic Law. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))
Metropolitan Transportation Authority: an abbreviation for a government agency, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A New York State law that, along with the Housing Maintenance Code, sets the requirements owners must follow to keep common areas and apartments in residential buildings safe and well maintained.

terms.term: MUTCD (Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices)
terms.def: The national standard, incorporated in federal regulations (23 CFR Part 655, Subpart F), for all traffic control devices (signs, signals, markings and other devices that regulate, warn or guide traffic) on any street, highway, bikeway, walkway, parking facility or private road open to public travel.

terms.term: NACTO (National Association of City Transportation Officials)
terms.def: A 501(c)(3) nonprofit that represents large cities on transportation issues and shares ideas, data and best practices. It publishes design guidance including the Urban Street Design Guide.
New Building: a DOB building/job type code, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

A formal determination that a proposed action will not have a significant adverse impact on the environment. A Negative Declaration means no Environmental Impact Statement is required and the project can move forward through other approvals.
A plan for a neighborhood's future that the community develops together.
Mesh with side ropes, ties and other parts, installed on scaffolding at construction sites, especially high-rises, to protect pedestrians and workers from falling debris.
A project for a permanent enclosed structure on a plot of land, with a roof and windows, used for any of many activities.
The City law regulating noise, including volume limits and times of day for activities such as music, construction and promotional events. Some violations go before the Environmental Control Board.

A building that predates and violates one or more current bulk rules, such as height or FAR. It may remain indefinitely and be changed if no new non-compliance is created or worsened, with special allowances for resiliency, accessibility, energy retrofits and residential conversions. If damaged or demolished, it can be rebuilt if at least 25 percent remains standing.

A non-complying building is any building that no longer complies with one or more of the bulk regulations of the applicable zoning district. The degree of non-compliance may not be increased. Regulations governing non-complying buildings can be found in Article V, Chapter 4, of the Zoning Resolution.

A lawfully existing building or structure that does not comply with applicable bulk regulations, either as of December 15, 1961 or because of a later zoning amendment. Non-compliance means failing to meet any bulk regulation.

A non-conforming use is any use that no longer conforms to one or more of the use regulations of the applicable zoning district. The degree of non- conformance may not be increased. Regulations governing non-conforming uses can be found in Article V, Chapters 2 and 3, of the Zoning Resolution.

A use that predates and does not conform with today's use rules, such as older housing in a Manufacturing District or a small store in a Residence District. It may remain indefinitely. If the space stays vacant more than two years, only conforming uses may re-occupy it, though small older shops in Residence Districts are exempt from that time limit.
Floors, countertops, walls and ceilings not used for food preparation but still regulated by the Health Department because they indirectly affect food safety.

The only legal way to evict a tenant for unpaid rent: a case in Housing Court that the owner may file three days after giving notice or making an oral demand for the rent. The tenant answers in person at the Housing Court Clerk's office and can present a defense to a judge.
The federal standard for classifying businesses. Since 2024, zoning uses NAICS to organize uses in Use Groups VI (Retail and Services) and X (Production).
A copy of a document signed by all parties before a Notary Public, who authenticates it so it can be relied on in later legal processes.
A notice the firm doing work that disturbs lead or unknown paint must file with DOHMH, where applicable, under Administrative Code section 27-2056.11(a)(2).

A notice issued when a business fails to comply with a law enforced by the Department of Consumer Affairs (DCWP). It explains how to settle or appear before an Administrative Law Judge to present a defense.

The notice HPD mails to the managing agent's business address registered with HPD (or to the owner if there is no managing agent) when a violation is issued. HPD also emails it if the owner gave an email address in the Property Registration. Heat and hot water violations are posted at the building at inspection.
No Plans: a DOB permit type code, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

In a holdover case, persistent and egregious conduct that threatens the health, safety or comfort of neighboring tenants. If the lease allows termination for nuisance, the owner must prove the tenant's behavior meets this standard.

terms.term: NYC Apartment Building Emergency Preparedness Guide
terms.def: An FDNY guide that the NYC Fire Code requires apartment building owners to prepare and distribute, with an annual bulletin and posted Close the Door notices, so residents know what to do in fire and non-fire emergencies.

The official DSNY trash bin required for properties with 1 to 9 residential units as of June 1, 2026. Trash sizes are 45, 35 and 25 gallons; compost sizes are 21 and 13 gallons. Sold at NYC Home Depot stores and via DoorDash, Instacart and Uber Eats.

The City agency that enforces the NYC Human Rights Law. Its Law Enforcement Bureau takes housing discrimination complaints, which must be filed within one year of the last act; reach it through 311 or its Infoline at (718) 722-3131.

The City's online portal to find and apply for affordable rental and homeownership opportunities, offered through a randomized lottery. Applicants must be at least 18 and meet income, household size, asset and other requirements, or have a voucher covering the rent.

The City law that makes it illegal to discriminate against a resident or housing applicant based on protected traits including race, national origin, immigration status, disability, presence of children, and lawful source of income (such as vouchers).

terms.term: NYC RR (New York City Report Recommendations)
terms.def: New York City Report Recommendations: an abbreviation DOB uses for a law, code or policy document, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

New York City Housing Authority, the city agency that owns and manages public housing developments. CB6 includes two NYCHA developments: Gowanus Houses (1,134 units) and Wyckoff Gardens (528 units). Both were central to the Gowanus rezoning negotiations.
An online map showing City data by geography (a geographic information system, GIS), offered as part of NYC Open Data.

terms.term: NYS ECL (New York State Environmental Conservation Law)
terms.def: New York State Environmental Conservation Law: an abbreviation DOB uses for a law, code or policy document, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

The New York State agency that oversees rent-regulated (rent-stabilized and rent-controlled) apartments. Owners register rents with HCR every year, and tenants can file complaints, ask about rent increases, or seek a rent reduction there (1-866-ASK-DHCR, 1-866-275-3427).
Outdoor Advertising Company: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Outdoor Advertising Sign: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

terms.term: OATH (Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings)
terms.def: Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Occupancy: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
The purpose or activity a building or space is used for, or is designed, arranged or intended to be used for.
The use as defined in the Building Code: the purpose or activity a building or space is used for, or is designed, arranged or intended to be used for.
The number of people a building's (or part of a building's) exits (means of egress) are designed for.

Required parking located on a separate lot within specified distances and districts, such as a Residence District site using parking in a Commercial District a block or two away. Not allowed in the Manhattan Core.
Rules setting how much parking a new development must provide, based on its location and proposed uses. Housing is calculated by number of dwelling units; retail by store square footage.

terms.term: Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings
terms.def: The City agency that hears and resolves challenges to violations issued by some City agencies, boards and commissions.

terms.term: Office of Child Support Enforcement Form
terms.def: A Human Resources Administration form for reporting child support responsibilities, which an individual must complete before applying for many NYC licenses and permits.
Overhead Protection: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A building designed and occupied for residence on a long-term basis (more than a month at a time) by no more than one family, as required by the Housing Maintenance Code.
An online portal with information on common New York State licenses businesses need.
DCP's website holding the official text of the Zoning Resolution, with search, clickable defined terms and cross references, section history buttons, and archived older versions.

Open space is the part of a residential zoning lot (which may include courts or yards) that is open and unobstructed from its lowest level to the sky, except for specific permitted obstructions, and accessible to and usable by all persons occupying dwelling units on the zoning lot. Depending upon the district, the amount of required open space is determined by the open space ratio, minimum yard regulations or by maximum lot coverage.

The open space ratio is the amount of open space required on a residential zoning lot in non-contextual districts, expressed as a percentage of the total floor area on the zoning lot. For example, if a building with 20,000 square feet of floor area has an OSR of 20, 4,000 square feet of open space would be required on the zoning lot (0.20 × 20,000 sq ft).

In Commercial and Manufacturing Districts uses generally must be in enclosed buildings, but zoning lets certain uses, or low-impact parts of them, occur outdoors, such as agriculture, outdoor skating rinks, restaurant outdoor dining and, in Manufacturing Districts, outdoor storage. Marked "U" in use group tables.
The speed drivers are observed traveling in free-flow conditions. The 85th percentile of observed speeds is the most common measure.
Operations Policy and Procedure Notice: an abbreviation DOB uses for a law, code or policy document, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
The court paper a tenant prepares at Housing Court to start an HP Action. It sets a date for the case and must be served on both the owner and HPD.
Other: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit), per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

Conditions placed on specific uses so they do not harm their surroundings, such as performance standards, limits on housing units or building types in some low-density districts, or required indoor waiting space for theaters in high-density commercial areas. Marked "P" in use group tables.
A parking area where zoning requires parking only for large residential developments and some non-residential developments. It is part of the Greater Transit Zone.

When occupants exceed the number on the Certificate of Occupancy or allowed by BC 1004.1. FDNY may also find a safety threat from the number of people, or from people sitting or standing where they block access to exits, aisles, corridors or stairways.

An overlay district is a district superimposed upon another district which supersedes, modifies or supplements the underlying regulations. Limited height districts and commercial overlay districts are examples of overlay districts.
Time worked beyond 40 hours a week, for which State law requires an employee be paid an additional amount.
An HPD office offering free classes for tenants and owners on topics such as homeownership, tenants' rights and DOB basics (212-863-8830).
Public Assembly: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Post Approval Amendment: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

A paired district matches an M1 district with an R3 through R10 district (M1- 5/R10, for example) to permit a mixture of residential and non-residential (commercial, community facility, light manufacturing) uses in the same zoning district, block or building. Paired districts are mapped in Special Mixed Use Districts and in the Special Long Island City Mixed Use District.

A parapet is a low wall or protective barrier that extends vertically above the roof of a building or other structure. A parapet wall that is no higher than four feet is a permitted obstruction and may penetrate a maximum height limit or required setback area.
A continuous extension of the exterior wall built entirely above the roof.
The standing of a vehicle, occupied or not, other than temporarily while actually loading or unloading property or passengers. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))

Rules that manage the flow of people and goods by setting how much off-street parking is required or allowed. More vehicle-dependent areas may have a minimum number of required spaces; transit-rich areas often have no minimum and may have a maximum instead.
Groupings of similar non-residential uses used to calculate how much parking each requires.
Parking requirements for commercial uses are grouped into nine parking requirement categories based on the compatibility of the uses and the amount of traffic generated.
A provision that removes calculated parking requirements for small lots or where the number of required spaces is small. Waivers vary by zoning district, parking area and use.

Construction that removes, replaces or repairs load-bearing or non-load-bearing interior partitions, changes structural elements inside or out, or changes the facade, while keeping the existing structure.

terms.term: PDC (New York City Public Design Commission)
terms.def: New York City Public Design Commission: an abbreviation for a government agency, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Professional Engineer: a DOB abbreviation for a construction professional, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

The hour or hours of greatest vehicle traffic volume on a street or intersection, usually defined for weekday AM, mid-day and PM, and Saturday mid-day peak periods. Traffic analyses typically study peak hours rather than a whole day.

A bicycle with fully operable pedals and an electric motor under 750 watts (one horsepower) that engages only while the rider pedals and the bike is under 20 miles per hour, and cuts out when the rider brakes, stops pedaling or reaches 20 mph. It may not have a throttle or other added motorized equipment. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))
Any person on foot or in a wheelchair. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 130)

An area designated by DOT for pedestrian circulation, use and enjoyment on property under DOT jurisdiction, such as a mapped public place or the bed of a roadway. It may include tables, seating, trees, plants, lighting, bike racks or public art. (NYC Administrative Code Section 19-157)

terms.term: Penalties for Work Without a Permit
terms.def: Doing work without a permit can lead to violations, court appearances and civil or criminal penalties. Some minor alterations, ordinary repairs, and replacing faucets, toilets and sinks need no permit and may be done by someone without a license (AC 28-105.4).
A performance standard is a minimum requirement or maximum allowable limit on noise, vibration, smoke, odor and other effects of industrial uses listed in Use Groups 17 and 18.

Limits on noise, air pollution and other nuisances that apply to a range of uses in Manufacturing Districts, such as food manufacturing and auto repair. More restrictive standards apply in light manufacturing districts than heavier ones.
Perimeter walls are the outermost walls of a building in a lower-density district that enclose floor area and rise from the base plane to a specified maximum height.

A permitted obstruction is a structure or object that may be located in a required yard or open space or penetrate a height limit, setback area or sky exposure plane. A balcony, trellis, air conditioner, gutter or fence is a permitted obstruction in required yards or open space. Certain structures on a roof, such as elevator bulkheads, water towers or parapets are permitted obstructions that may penetrate height limits, setback areas or sky exposure planes.

All non-required accessory parking a site may voluntarily provide, subject to maximums. South of Central Park, spaces are limited to 20 percent of dwelling units and never more than 200; elsewhere up to two spaces per dwelling unit in a multiple dwelling, and never more than 200.
Rectangular or semicircular projections from a wall that reinforce it or act as simulated pillars at entrances and doorways; they may also project from the exterior wall.
Public Information Panel: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

The envelope required for single- and two-family houses in lowest-density districts that require side yards. The perimeter wall may be up to 25 feet; above that the building must slope inward and never exceed 35 feet.
Plumbing: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit) and a DOB permit type code, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

Occupancy classifications for gatherings of 75 people or more for civic, social or religious functions, recreation, eating or drinking, awaiting transportation or similar group activities. A Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation is required.

terms.term: Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation (PACO)
terms.def: After plans are approved under BC 1028.1.3 and DOB inspection is passed, an initial PACO is issued for one year. After that, an annual FDNY inspection is required to renew it (FC 105.6).
The step in a permit or license application where drawings are reviewed to confirm a space complies with rules. In DOB's BISWeb, "P/E" means an application is in Plan Examination.

A project cannot begin until its plans are reviewed and approved by a DOB Plan Examiner, or accepted if Professionally Certified. Disapproved applications get objections that must be resolved before approval; the design professional schedules appointments with examiners to resolve them.
A common class of DOB applications for changing a space's use or shape. For example, a PW-1 is needed for renovation and a PW-6 for a new Certificate of Occupancy.

Special rules for four planned communities (Parkchester, Harlem River Houses, Fresh Meadows and Sunnyside Gardens) where demolition, construction or landscape alteration is not allowed as-of-right and needs City Planning Commission approval.

Planting strips are grassy areas that extend along the edge of the curb within which street trees are planted in R1 through R5 districts. Planting strips are a required streetscape improvement in certain districts.

A raised area in a building for worship, music, plays or entertainment, a head table, lecturers and speakers, boxing and wrestling rings, theater-in-the-round and similar uses, with no overhead curtains, drops, scenery or stage effects other than lighting and sound. A temporary platform is installed for no more than 30 days.
Keeping ingredients in a refrigerator at the food preparation area so they stay as cold as needed throughout preparation.
Pointing is the mortar in the joints between bricks, stone and other masonry units; repointing is removing old mortar and replacing it with new.
A formal determination that a proposed action may have significant adverse environmental impacts. A Positive Declaration triggers the requirement for a full Environmental Impact Statement (EIS).

Any food that can support growth of dangerous microorganisms, such as raw and cooked animal products (like meat and milk) and cooked starches (like potatoes and rice). A HACCP plan may be used to reduce risks.

terms.term: Power of Attorney / Authority to Act
terms.def: Legal permission, set out in a legal document, for one person to act on behalf of another, often to manage documents for them.
Policy and Procedure Notice: an abbreviation DOB uses for a law, code or policy document, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

The period before a ULURP application is officially certified by DCP and the public review clock starts. DCP may require community engagement, environmental review, or other steps during pre-certification. CB6 often engages with applicants during this phase.
A DOB violation where a Notice of Violation, administrative summons, criminal court summons or other process was issued before the initial work permit was issued.

terms.term: Pre-Permit / Pre-Operational Health Inspections or Consultations
terms.def: A Health Department consultation for restaurants not yet open, confirming compliance with health laws. It carries no operating fines and helps a restaurant open faster. See also Inspection Cycle.

A predominantly built-up area is a blockfront entirely within an R4 or R5 district (without a suffix) in which optional regulations that permit higher floor area ratios and lower parking requirements may be used to produce infill housing. At least 50 percent of the area of the block must be occupied by zoning lots developed with buildings, and the zoning lot that will be developed with infill housing may not exceed 1.5 acres (65,340 sq ft). Infill regulations may not be used to redevelop a lot occupied by a one- or two-family detached or semi- detached house unless the blockfront is predominantly developed with attached or multifamily housing.
The part of a lease where the owner prohibits certain activities in the space, which may bar the tenant from things that would otherwise be legal.
A company that hauls waste for businesses.

A private road is a right-of-way that gives vehicular access to developments with five or more dwelling units that are located at least 50 feet from a public street in R1 through R5 districts. Developments on private roads must comply with special design rules. In lower density growth management areas, a right- of-way that provides access to three or more dwelling units is a private road.

A privately owned public space is an amenity provided and maintained by the property owner for public use, usually in exchange for additional floor area. Located mainly in the high-density, central business districts of Manhattan, these spaces are typically in the form of an arcade or a public plaza with seating and landscaping and may be located within or outside a building.
Permit: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A process letting a licensed architect or engineer self-approve projects without initial DOB review.
A person licensed by New York State to design or evaluate building spaces under applicable rules. PEs often work with registered architects and contractors.

Submitting construction documents prepared by a registered design professional (Professional Engineer or Registered Architect) to DOB for approval. In some cases, with the owner's consent, the professional may self-certify Code compliance (professional certification) instead of DOB review.

To close a permit, the owner, applicant or contractor must have the finished work inspected for final sign-off and submit a work completion notification to DOB. In some cases a letter of completion may be issued.
The legal boundary (metes and bounds) of a parcel of land.

terms.term: Property Tax and Interest Deferral (PTAID) Program
terms.def: A City program homeowners can apply to for help with property taxes; named in the guide as a resource the Homeowner Help Desk helps homeowners access.
Partial Stop Work Order: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A meeting before a government decision-making body where anyone can comment on a proposal.
Any highway, road, street, avenue, alley, public place, public driveway or other public way. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 134)
A DSNY-serviced corner basket for pedestrians' light trash only, found on commercial corners and near transit hubs. Household and commercial waste are not allowed.
An announcement the law requires, often in widely read newspapers, a set number of days before a public hearing or upcoming action.

A public park is any publicly owned park, playground, beach, parkway, or roadway within the jurisdiction and control of the New York City Commissioner of Parks & Recreation. Typically, public parks are not subject to zoning regulations.

A public parking garage is a building or part of a building that is used on a daily basis for public parking. A public parking garage may include some accessory off-street parking spaces for uses on the same zoning lot.
A public parking lot is a tract of land that is used on a daily basis for public parking and is not accessory to a use on the same or another zoning lot.

A public plaza is a privately owned open area adjacent to a building and accessible to the public. It must generally be at the level of the sidewalk it adjoins and be unobstructed to the sky except for seating and other permitted amenities. In certain high-density zoning districts, a floor area bonus is available for the provision of a public plaza.

terms.term: Public Realm Improvement Fund Governing Group
terms.def: A group set up by zoning in East Midtown to administer a fund for public realm improvement projects; members include government agencies, elected officials, community boards and civic groups.
The public street space beyond the private property line, including roadway and sidewalk.
Open space outside a building that is dedicated to public use by lawful mapping or another lawful procedure.
Qualified Exterior Wall Inspector: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A defined term central to UAP that includes UAP developments. It is allowed a higher FAR (for example 3.9 instead of 3.0 in R6A) and higher maximum height than standard housing.

A ground floor of a development or enlargement of a Quality Housing building, where the start of the second story is 13 feet or more above the level of the sidewalk and, in certain instances, where additional supplementary use provisions are met. In some zoning districts, buildings with a Qualifying Ground Floor are permitted a higher maximum base and overall height.

Created in 2024, a defined term listing size and location conditions under which a lot in a lower-density district can use special use, bulk and parking rules to allow "missing middle" apartment buildings at the scale of older buildings. See ZR Section 12-10.

The Quality Housing Program, mandatory in contextual R6 through R10 residence districts and optional in non-contextual R6 through R10 districts, encourages development consistent with the character of many established neighborhoods. Its bulk regulations set height limits and allow high lot coverage buildings that are set at or near the street line. The Quality Housing Program also requires amenities relating to interior space, recreation areas and landscaping.

Residence Districts created in 2024 with the city's highest residential densities (15 and 18 FAR). They can only be mapped in Mandatory Inclusionary Housing areas; first applied in Midtown South. Contextual and Commercial District versions exist.

terms.term: R2A, R3A, R3X, R4A, R4-1 and R5A
terms.def: In R2A, R3A, R3X, R4A, R4-1 and R5A districts, if the adjacent front yards are deeper than the minimum required front yard, a new building must provide a front yard at least as deep as one of the adjacent yards, but it need not be deeper than 20 feet.

In R4B, R5B and R5D districts, if the adjacent front yards are deeper than the minimum required front yard, then the front yard of a new building must be at least as deep as one adjacent front yard and no deeper than the other, but it need not be deeper than 20 feet.

In R6A, R7A, 7D and R7X districts, the street wall of a new building may be located no closer to the street line than the street wall of any building within 150 feet on the same blockfront, but need not be located farther from the street line than 15 feet.

In R6B, R7B and R8B districts, the street wall of a new building, on any lot up to 50 feet wide, must be as deep as one adjacent wall and no deeper than the other. On lots wider than 50 feet, the street wall of a new building may be no closer to the street line than the street wall of an adjacent building. A street wall need not be located farther from the street line than 15 feet.
Registered Architect: a DOB abbreviation for a construction professional, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

Railroad or transit air space is space directly over an open railroad or transit right-of-way or yard in existence on or after September 27, 1962. Development may be permitted only by CPC special permit.
A planted depression that captures and absorbs rainwater that would otherwise flow into a storm drain, mainly through infiltration and evapotranspiration.
An exhaust system for hot air required for large commercial stoves. Range hoods need special permits from the Fire Department.
Request for Corrective Action: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

terms.term: RCNY (Rules of the City of New York)
terms.def: Rules of the City of New York: an abbreviation DOB uses for a law, code or policy document, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A New York State law protecting tenants' right to form, join and take part in tenant associations to protect their rights to repairs and services.
Open area required on through lots, which have no rear lot line, to match the rear yards of more typical lots. It can often be placed elsewhere on the lot.

Space, indoors or outdoors and accessible to all residents, that new apartment buildings with nine or more units must provide, equal to three percent of residential floor area (for example a rooftop patio or basement gym).
A type of backflow prevention device reliable enough for restaurant kitchen uses, but not for bathroom or other high-hazard business uses, as required by law. See also Backflow Prevention Device.

Created in 2021, a consistent level set 10 feet above grade from which owners in the highest-risk floodplain areas may measure height limits, to support resiliency improvements. Buildings using it must follow strict flood-resistant construction standards. See Article VI, Chapter 4.
A person licensed by New York State to design and submit drawings for construction and interior layouts.
A person licensed and registered to practice land surveying under New York State education law.
The HPD unit that helps owners with Annual Property Registration, at 100 Gold Street, 6th floor (212-863-7000, register@hpd.nyc.gov).
Remedy: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

Changes to an existing building, such as remodeling or replacing outdated or damaged structures and materials, partial demolition of interior partitions, and installing or replacing building systems or equipment as regular maintenance. Renovations do not affect exits, change the use, or increase the occupant load.
The HCR-approved form a rent-stabilized owner uses to offer a tenant a renewal lease of one or two years, at the tenant's choice, at the rate set by the Rent Guidelines Board.
The board whose approvals set the allowable rent increases for rent-stabilized lease renewals. Renewal leases are offered at the rate the Rent Guidelines Board sets.

An apartment covered by rent stabilization or rent control. Tenants in these apartments have additional rights, such as regulated lease renewals and limits on rent increases. Tenants can check whether an apartment or building is registered as rent-regulated by calling HCR at 718-739-6400 or emailing rentinfo@nycshr.org.
The committee approved the bill by majority vote and sent it on to the full Council for a final vote at a Stated meeting.
Required: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

A residence consists of one or more dwelling units or rooming units, and any common areas, including one-family and two-family houses, multifamily dwellings or apartment hotels. A single-family residence* is a building on a zoning lot containing one dwelling unit occupied by one household. A two-family residence* is a building on a zoning lot containing two dwelling units occupied by two households. In R3-1, R3A, R3X, R4-1 and R4A districts, two-family houses, both detached and semi-detached, must have at least 75% of one dwelling unit directly above or below the other. A multifamily residence is a building on a zoning lot containing at least three dwelling units.
A residence district, designated by the letter R (R3-2, R5, R10A, for example), is a zoning district in which only residences and community facilities are permitted.
The places where people live, from row houses to high rises, built of brick, concrete and stone.

A residential district equivalent is a residential district designation assigned to a C1, C2, C3, C4, C5 or C6 district that establishes the regulations for residential development within the district. Any residential development in a C4-4 district, for example, must follow the bulk regulations of its residential equivalent, an R7 district.
The Residence District whose residential bulk rules apply to housing in a given Commercial District, for example R6A for a C4-2A district.

Building Code: Group R is use for dwelling or sleeping; three or more units make a multiple dwelling under the Multiple Dwelling Law; stays may be transient (30 days or less) or non-transient. Zoning Resolution: a building with one or more dwelling or rooming units, excluding hotels and community facilities with sleeping space; also a district type where hotels are not allowed.
A residential use is any use listed in Use Group 1 (single-family detached residences) or Use Group 2 (all other types of residential development).

The ability of people, places and infrastructure (such as transportation and energy) to withstand a stress or shock, recover and emerge stronger. In the Manual it refers to climate threats: sea-level rise, coastal storms, extreme precipitation and heat.
A legally mapped street permanently closed to motor vehicles by DOT and open to pedestrians. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-12(r)(4))

A recorded legal covenant that binds current and future property owners to specific conditions, mitigation requirements, environmental remediation, or other obligations tied to a project approval. It runs with the land.

A wall that holds back soil between two elevations, resisting lateral forces from soil, rock, water or other materials (BC 1801.3). Basement walls and vault walls of buildings and underground structures, such as utility vaults, tunnels and transit stations, are not retaining walls.
The Mayor let the 30-day window pass without signing or vetoing the Council-passed bill, so it became law automatically without a signature.
Under City Charter Chapter 14, Section 362(d), a right the City can revoke at any time, allowing private use or improvements on, over or under City streets and sidewalks. DOT has jurisdiction.

A rezoning or remapping occurs when the zoning designation(s) for an area is changed on the zoning map to facilitate policy initiatives, such as preserving neighborhoods and promoting economic development around transit hubs. A zoning map amendment is subject to the ULURP review process.
A general term for land, property or interest in it, usually a strip, acquired for or devoted to transportation.
Plastic that is relatively inflexible and keeps its shape when bent, such as food and drink containers, caps, lids and cups. Recyclable regardless of the number on it.
An open way on land for the passage of vehicles, people or animals.
The graded portion of a highway within its top and side slopes, prepared as a foundation for the pavement and shoulder.
The portion of a street designed, improved or ordinarily used for vehicle travel, not including the shoulder and slope. (RCNY Title 34, Section 2-01)
Report: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Reference Standard: an abbreviation DOB uses for a law, code or policy document and an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Sidewalk: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A notice owners of multiple dwellings must distribute and post when they apply for a permit for work beyond minor alterations or ordinary repairs.
Cleaning an object or area to reduce harmful microorganisms to an acceptable level; a term often used in Health Department rules.

New York City's version of Bus Rapid Transit, connecting neighborhoods with limited transit options to subway stations and major destinations. Tools include off-board fare payment, bus lanes, Transit Signal Priority and longer spacing between stops.
Safe Construction Bill of Rights: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A formal document listing conditions or materials that must be approved or used for a project to proceed or a permit to be approved.

The process by which the lead agency and the public define the range of issues and alternatives to be studied in a Draft EIS. CB6 can participate in scoping to ensure relevant neighborhood concerns, like flooding, traffic, or historic resources, are included.

Marking concrete's surface for visual or texture effect. "Tooled joint" scoring finishes sidewalk flag joints with a hand-troweled border; "simulated saw-cut joint" scoring uses a spacer to mimic joints cut with a masonry saw.
Standpipe: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit), per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A lid that closes fully so the bin contains waste and keeps pests out. Required on trash, recycling and compost bins, which must hold 55 gallons or less.

A door that, when opened and released, returns to the closed position and latches by itself. All apartment doors and doors in and leading to public halls should be self-closing, to keep fire and smoke from spreading through the building.

Starting July 2023, HPD proactively inspects 300 buildings a year, identified from HPD, DOB and FDNY data, and issues violations for self-closing doors in common areas, hallways and corridors without waiting for tenant complaints.

A program that freezes the rent of eligible tenants 62 or older and exempts them from future increases. The household must earn $50,000 or less, pay more than one-third of income in rent, and live in a rent-controlled, rent-stabilized or hotel-stabilized apartment as a named tenant or with succession rights.

New York State Environmental Quality Review Act, state law requiring all government agencies to assess environmental impacts of discretionary actions before approving them. CEQR is New York City's local implementation. Applies to rezonings, special permits, and other discretionary approvals.
The minimum distance a building must step back from the street above its base height. Deeper setbacks are required on narrow streets. After the setback the building can rise to its maximum height.

A setback is the portion of a building that is set back above the base height (or street wall or perimeter wall) before the total height of the building is achieved. The position of a building setback in height factor districts is controlled by sky exposure planes and, in contextual districts, by specified distances from street walls.

terms.term: Setbacks, Front Yard or Ground Level
terms.def: Front yards are required in R1 through R5 districts; rules governing the depth of open areas at ground level between the front building wall and the street line apply in R6 through R10 districts. Front yards and open areas must be planted and have a minimum depth that meets the following requirements:

Placing trash, recycling or compost at the curb for DSNY collection. Rules set when you may set out (after 6:00 PM, or 8:00 PM for bags at 10+ unit buildings), what container to use, and that all waste should be out by midnight.
Scaffold: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit), per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Sign: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit), per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
The City law regulating emission of pollutants and other harmful substances into the air.
Sidewalk Shed: a DOB permit type code, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

An enclosed space running through one or more stories (or to the roof) connecting a series of openings, whether for air, light, elevator, dumbwaiter, enclosed stairway or other purpose, interior or exterior.
A food preparation facility giving food retailers or preparers access to shared equipment. Operators must be permitted by the Health Department.

A bikeway physically separated from motor vehicle traffic by open space or a barrier, within a highway right-of-way or its own right-of-way. Pedestrians, skaters, wheelchair users, joggers and other non-motorized users may also use it.

A side lot ribbon is an 8 to 10 foot wide strip that extends along the length of the side lot line of a zoning lot. It is not required to be open to the sky and can extend through an attached house set along the side lot line. In R3, R4 and R5 districts, if a zoning lot is less than 35 feet wide, parking must be located in a side lot ribbon.

Sidewalk cafe A sidewalk cafe is a portion of an eating or drinking establishment that is located on a public sidewalk. Sidewalk cafe regulations are administered by the Department of Consumer Affairs. An enclosed sidewalk cafe* is a sidewalk cafe that is contained within a structure. An unenclosed sidewalk cafe* contains readily removable tables, chairs or railings, with no overhead coverage other than umbrellas or a retractable awning. A small sidewalk cafe* is an unenclosed sidewalk cafe containing no more than a single row of tables and chairs in a space no greater than 4½ feet from the street line, with no barrier between the café and the sidewalk.

The portion of a street, paved or unpaved, between the curb or roadway edge and adjacent property lines, intended for pedestrians. Where unclear, it is the area between the building line and the curb. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))
Any covered space below a sidewalk and/or street, except openings used only for steps down to a building's cellar or basement.
A requirement along certain streets that new buildings set back and extend the sidewalk onto their property by a defined number of feet to handle pedestrian traffic.

A sign is any writing, words, pictures or symbols, that is on or attached to a building or other structure. An accessory sign* directs attention to a business, profession, commodity, service or entertainment conducted, sold or offered upon the same zoning lot. An advertising sign* directs attention to a business, profession, commodity, service or entertainment conducted, sold or offered on a different zoning lot. A flashing sign* is any illuminated sign, whether stationary, revolving or rotating, which changes light or color. An illuminated sign* uses artificial light or reflected light from an artificial source.

Zoning rules on sign type, size, illumination and location. Residence Districts allow mainly small unlit nameplates and identification signs. In C1 and C2 districts a sign may equal three times the street frontage, up to a maximum of 150 square feet, with each storefront calculating from its own frontage.
Rules that define where a building can be placed on a site, such as yards and lot coverage. They differ based on whether the zoning lot is a corner, through or interior lot.
An official drawing showing a planned space and its surroundings, such as sidewalk, neighboring buildings, parking or street front. See also Floor Plans.

A Site Safety Plan is required for major buildings, including new buildings, alterations and demolitions 10 stories or more, and facade work on buildings 15 stories or more (BC 3310). It details construction logistics protecting public areas and neighbors, such as fences, sidewalk sheds, adjoining buildings and safety netting (AC 28-110.1).

A limit on the size of a use, by square footage or number of seats, so it fits its district. For example, clothing and department stores cannot exceed 10,000 square feet in neighborhood commercial districts. Limits apply to individual businesses, not the total of the use on a lot. Marked "S" in use group tables.

A sketch map is an illustration of a proposed change to the Zoning Map or the City Map that provides a graphic, easy to read version of the change. The sketch map is attached to the Notice of Certification (NOC) when an application for a Zoning Map or City Map change is certified as complete by the Department of City Planning and distributed for public review. Sketch maps are limited in scope and scale to include only the area affected by the proposed action and do not necessarily reflect the final action.

A sky exposure plane is a virtual sloping plane that begins at a specified height above the street line and rises inward over the zoning lot at a ratio of vertical distance to horizontal distance set forth in district regulations. A building may not penetrate the sky exposure plane which is designed to provide light and air at street level, primarily in medium- and higher-density districts.

A tall building or enlargement that is 45 feet wide or less, in an R7-2, R7X, R8, R9 or R10 district, is commonly called a sliver building. Such buildings are generally restricted to a height equal to the width of the abutting street or 100 feet, whichever is less.
Public food scrap drop-off bins open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, unlocked with the free NYC Compost app. They accept food scraps, food-soiled paper and plant waste.
The pile of snow plows leave at the end of a driveway, which residents must clear.
Support of Excavation: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A business owned and run by one person, which files paperwork and taxes differently from other businesses.
An action to prevent pollution where it originates.
Stopping and/or reducing pollutants at their point of generation so they do not come into contact with stormwater.
Sprinkler: a DOB work type code (the kind of work on a permit), per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

A temporary or permanent building for amusement, entertainment or education with a walkway, or a ride that carries passengers around or over a course (for example haunted houses, laser tag arenas, mazes). Exits may not be obvious because of visual or audio distractions or an intentionally confusing path.

Inspections of selected materials, equipment, installation, fabrication and connections to confirm they match approved construction documents and standards. Only DOB-registered Special Inspection Agencies (SIAs), their representatives or qualified professionals may perform them.

Short for Special Purpose District. A zoning layer that the City Planning Commission maps over the underlying districts to achieve specific planning and urban-design goals in a defined area. Its rules modify, supplement, or override the base zoning, and where they conflict the special-district rules control. On the city zoning map these appear as a special district code. The one mapped in CB6 is the Special Gowanus Mixed Use District (code G).

The special purpose district created by the 2021 Gowanus rezoning. It pairs residential and light-manufacturing (M1) districts so housing and industry can sit side by side, and is organized into five subdistricts with their own rules. It layers Mandatory Inclusionary Housing onto mapped areas, treats blocks along the Gowanus Canal as waterfront subject to a Waterfront Access Plan, and adds environmental, ground-floor, and streetscape requirements on top of the base zoning. Found in the NYC Zoning Resolution, Article XIII, Chapter 9.
A Special Purpose District with number suffixes (MX-4, MX-8, etc.) that pairs a Residence District with a Manufacturing District and sets how the two sets of rules work together.

A discretionary approval that allows modification of use, bulk, or parking rules when specific findings are met. Some special permits go through the City Planning Commission via ULURP; others go to the BSA. CB6 reviews and votes on CPC special permits.

The regulations for special purpose districts are designed to supplement and modify the underlying zoning in order to respond to distinctive neighborhoods with particular issues and goals. Special purpose districts are shown as overlays on the zoning maps and are in Articles VIII–XIII of the Resolution.

A split lot is a zoning lot located in two or more zoning districts and divided by a zoning district boundary. In most cases, zoning regulations for each district must be applied separately for each portion of the lot. Special rules for zoning lots that existed prior to 1961, or prior to any rezoning that splits a lot, can be found in Article VII, Chapter 7, of the Zoning Resolution.
Single Room Occupancy: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
The federal application for an Employer Identification Number, required for filing taxes. Sole proprietorships are exempt. See also Employer Identification Number.
Site Safety Coordinator: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Site Safety Manager: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Site Safety Training: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Structural: a DOB permit type code, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A space in a building for entertainment or presentations that has overhead curtains, drops, scenery or stage effects other than lighting and sound.
Stopping a vehicle, occupied or not, other than temporarily while actually receiving or discharging passengers. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 145; RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))
The State agency that oversees the sale of alcoholic beverages in New York State.
Any halting of a vehicle, even momentarily, whether occupied or not. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))
Temporary, seasonal vestibules allowed as supplementary building entrances.
The abnormal rise of water generated by a storm, over and above the predicted astronomical tides.
Storm water from all water-resistant surfaces on a property must drain into a public storm or combined sewer, or an on-site private disposal system such as a drywell.
A story is that part of a building between the surface of one floor and the ceiling immediately above. A cellar does not count as a story.
Covers or locking knobs for gas stoves that keep young children from turning on the gas. Owners must provide them where a child under six lives, or on request.

A street is any road (other than a private road), highway, parkway, avenue, alley or other way shown on the City Map, or a way at least 50 feet wide and intended for public use which connects a way shown on the City Map to another such way or to a building or structure. A street refers to the entire public right-of-way (including public sidewalks). A narrow street* is a street that is less than 75 feet wide. A wide street* is a street that is 75 feet or more in width. Most bulk regulations applicable to wide streets are also applicable to buildings on intersecting streets within 100 feet of a wide street.
A street line is a front lot line separating the zoning lot from the street.
A tree growing in the public right-of-way. Street trees provide benefits ranging from higher property values to stormwater capture and urban heat island relief.

Most new buildings must provide street trees along the sidewalk; in low-density Residence Districts a planting strip along the curb is also required. The Department of Parks and Recreation can exempt sites where sidewalk planting is not possible.
A street wall is a wall or portion of a wall of a building facing a street.

A citywide framework adopted in 2024 for the ground floors of buildings in Commercial Districts, replacing a patchwork of earlier rules. It has three levels, Tiers A, B and C, with stricter design standards at each tier.

The lightest streetscape rules, for commercial streets far from transit: limits on blank walls and where parking spaces can go on the lot. Areas near highway ramps and large shopping complexes are exempt.

Streetscape rules for major commercial corridors near transit. They restrict ground floor apartments and infrastructure uses, limit residential lobbies (under 50 feet wide), amenities, parking and loading, and require part of the ground floor to have windows (transparency).

The strictest streetscape rules, applied on specified streets (for example in some Special Purpose Districts and many Manhattan avenues). They require commercial use continuity, limit residential lobbies to under 25 feet wide, and bar parking lots, curb cuts and loading docks.
Industrial by-products used in concrete that would otherwise go to landfills, saving manufacturers money and reducing environmental impact.
Reducing pollution and waste to make the city a green, healthy place.
Stop Work Order: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Sidewalk Shed: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Size: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

The speed vehicles should travel on a street given the level of walking, biking and other activity generated by adjacent land uses, balancing vehicle mobility with safety for pedestrians and cyclists. It is usually the posted speed limit.
A unique number for each block in New York City, used to track information about the block, such as taxes.
A tax lot is a parcel of land identified with a unique borough, block and lot number for property tax purposes. A zoning lot comprises one or more adjacent tax lots within a block.

terms.term: Taxation and Finance, New York State Department of
terms.def: The State agency that oversees taxes and finance in New York State, including sales and property taxes.
An identifying number the IRS uses for tax purposes. See also Employer Identification Number.
Table: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Temporary Certificate of Occupancy: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Temporary: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
A network of devices deployed on surfaces to reduce flood impacts to buildings, roadways and other assets.

terms.term: Tenant Data Privacy Law (Local Law 63 of 2021)
terms.def: A City law covering multiple dwellings that use keyless smart access systems (key fobs, apps, biometrics and similar). Owners must give tenants a data retention and privacy policy, protect the data, and not misuse the system to track or harass tenants.

Illegal conduct by an owner to force tenants out or make them give up their rights, such as unjustified eviction notices, illegal lockouts, threats, overcharging rent, failing to make repairs or provide utilities, improper buyout offers, or deliberately causing construction problems.
A task force that takes complaints directly (email THPT@hpd.nyc.gov) when harassment takes the form of construction or a lack of basic services, repairs or utilities.
A City helpline, reached by calling 311, that gives tenants facing harassment or at risk of losing their apartment legal assistance, City agency referrals and community resources.

A notice meeting section 120.1.3 of the NYC Administrative Code that owners must give to each occupied unit and post until permitted work is complete, in English and as necessary in Spanish, Arabic, Haitian Creole, Chinese, Korean and Russian.

A council set up by zoning in the Theater District that uses a zoning-established fund to promote theater and theater-related uses. Members include City representatives, elected officials and theater industry representatives.
Any lot that touches two parallel streets and is not a corner lot. Through lots have no rear lot line and instead must provide "rear yard equivalents."
Vehicle traffic whose trip origin and destination are not in the immediate area of a given street.
HPD's online appointment system for booking a phone or Microsoft Teams appointment with Code Enforcement about complaints and violations, or with the Registration Assistance Unit about registration.
The amount below minimum wage an employer may pay a waiter or other service worker for hours serving tipping customers, expected to be made up by tips so the worker still earns the full minimum wage.

A tower is a portion of a building that penetrates the sky exposure plane and is allowed only in specified high-density areas of the city. A tower may be occupied by residential, commercial or community facility uses. The standard tower rules generally permit the tower portion of a building to cover no more than 40 percent of the area of the zoning lot, or up to 50 percent on lots smaller than 20,000 square feet. The tower portion of a building must be set back at least 10 feet from a wide street and at least 15 feet from a narrow street. These regulations are modified for different uses and districts. A tower-on-a-base requires a contextual base between 60 and 85 feet high that extends continuously along the street line. The height of the tower is con- trolled by a minimum lot coverage requirement and a rule that at least 55 percent of the floor area on the zoning lot be located below a height of 150 feet. On a wide street in R9 and R10 districts and their C1 or C2 equivalents, a building that includes a residential tower must comply with tower-on-a-base regulations in addition to the standard tower rules.
Tenant Protection Plan: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Technical Policy and Procedure Notice: an abbreviation DOB uses for a law, code or policy document, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Technical Report: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Pedestrians, ridden or herded animals, vehicles, bicycles and other conveyances, singly or together, using any highway for travel. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 152)

Speed management that supports the livability of residential and commercial areas by improving safety, mobility and comfort for non-motorists, usually by reducing vehicle speeds or volumes. Measures include horizontal, vertical, lane narrowing and roadside interventions and other self-enforcing physical or perceptual features.
All signs, signals, markings and devices placed by a public body or official with jurisdiction to regulate, warn or guide traffic. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 153)

The ability to transfer unused development rights from a landmark site to a receiving lot. TDRs are commonly used to compensate landmark owners who cannot build to their full FAR while allowing a neighboring site to build larger. Requires LPC and CPC approval.

Space on a development site next to a train station that the transit agency may request for station improvements, such as an elevator. Floor space in a transit easement volume is exempt from floor area and extra height may be allowed. Rules are in Article VI, Chapter 6.

An area where special lower accessory parking requirements apply for various types of affordable housing including income-restricted housing units. These are generally areas of the city beyond the Manhattan Core within one- half mile of a subway station where auto ownership rates are among the lowest in the city.
The ways people get around the city, including subways, buses and bikes.
Items that cannot be recycled or composted and do not need special handling.

Except as otherwise specified in RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b), any vehicle or combination of vehicles designed to transport property that has either two axles and six tires, or three or more axles. (RCNY Title 34, Section 4-13(a))

Lead-safety work Local Law 1 requires when an apartment changes tenants, done by certified contractors before the new tenant moves in, whether or not the new tenant has a child. Turnover violations apply to all window and door friction surfaces in the apartment.
A building designed and occupied for residence on a long-term basis (more than a month at a time) by no more than two families, as required by the Housing Maintenance Code.

Created in 2024, a defined term for buildings meeting strict energy standards, which may take a five percent floor area deduction. Requirements differ for new and existing buildings. See ZR Section 12-10.

The Uniform Land Use Review Procedure, the city's formal public review process for major land use actions including rezonings, special permits, acquisitions, dispositions, and city map changes. ULURP gives CB6 a 60-day window to hold a public hearing and issue an advisory recommendation.

An HPD program that each year selects 50 to 100 buildings with many mold and leak problems and orders the owner to have a professional find the cause and fix the conditions and related violations within four months.

The baseline rules of a zoning district found in Articles II, III and IV. They are called "underlying" because they may be, and often are, modified or superseded by Special Purpose Districts or rules for geographically specific areas.
A program all employers pay taxes into that provides income to workers who lose their jobs through no fault of their own. See also Insurance.

See ULURP. The formal public review sequence: Community Board (60 days) → Borough President (30 days) → City Planning Commission (60 days) → City Council (50 days) → Mayor (5 days). CB6's vote is advisory but part of the official record.
A paving material that is precast (such as a hexagonal asphalt paver) or individually cut (such as a granite block), so each piece can be removed or replaced individually.

Created in 2024, a program giving permanently affordable and supportive housing a higher FAR than other housing in all medium- and high-density districts that allow housing where MIH does not apply. Applicants work with HPD on an affordable housing plan. See ZR Section 12-10 and Article II, Chapter 7.
The design of the city that shapes public space, so people feel at home wherever they go.

The phenomenon where urban and suburban areas are hotter than surrounding rural areas. A city of one million or more people can average 1.8 to 5.4 degrees F (1 to 3 degrees C) warmer, and on a clear, calm night the difference can reach 22 degrees F (12 degrees C).

A use is any activity, occupation, business or operation, listed in Use Groups 1 through 18, or identified in a special permit, which is conducted in a building or on a tract of land. Certain uses are allowed only by special permit of the CPC or BSA.

The NYC Zoning Resolution organizes permitted uses into numbered groups (UG 1 through UG 18). Each zoning district permits certain use groups. For example, residential districts permit UG 1–4; manufacturing districts permit UGs up to 18.

Rules on where uses may go within a building. In neighborhood commercial districts, commercial uses are limited to the lower two stories, with extra restrictions where commercial and residential uses share the second story. In central business districts commercial uses may be on any story, with limited allowances above residences.

Rules setting out where different kinds of activities may be located in the city. They sort out which uses belong together in each district so that activities that do not mix well, such as polluting factories and homes, are not permitted in the same district.
The period an asset or component is expected to be available for use, assuming regular and adequate maintenance.

Relief from zoning rules granted where strict compliance would create practical difficulty or hardship. For area variances (bulk), all five findings under ZR §72-21 must be proven. Granted by the Board of Standards and Appeals, not the CPC.

Every device in, upon or by which a person or property is or may be transported or drawn on a highway, except devices moved by human power or used only on stationary rails or tracks. (NYS Vehicle and Traffic Law Section 159; RCNY Title 34, Section 4-01(b))
Upward displacement of moving vehicles by raising the road surface, for example with a hump, table or other raised element. A traffic calming technique.
The Mayor formally rejected a bill the Council passed. The Council can still make it law by overriding the veto with a two-thirds vote of its members.

New York City's action plan to improve street safety in every neighborhood and borough, combining expanded enforcement against dangerous moving violations like speeding and failing to yield, new street designs, public outreach, and a legislative agenda to raise penalties for dangerous drivers and give NYC control over its own streets.
With: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Without: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Money paid to a worker, regulated differently by City, State and federal governments.
A separate sink only for washing pots, pans and dishes, not hands or raw food. It must connect to special plumbing that captures grease before wastewater enters the sewer. See also Hand-Wash Sink.
Where the city meets the water. New York City has 520 miles of waterfront.
