A waterfront access plan is a detailed framework set forth in the Zoning Resolution, that tailors waterfront bulk regulations and public access requirements to the specific conditions of a particular waterfront. Development of individual waterfront parcels governed by the plan triggers a requirement to build and maintain public access areas in accordance with the WAP.

A waterfront area is the geographical area adjacent to a body of water at least 100 feet wide, comprising all blocks between the pierhead line and a parallel line 800 feet landward from the shoreline. Blocks within the waterfront area are subject to waterfront zoning regulations. The bulkhead line is a line shown on the zoning maps which divides the upland and seaward portions of waterfront zoning lots. The pierhead line is a line shown on the zoning maps which defines the outermost seaward boundary of the area regulated by the Zoning Resolution. The shoreline* is the mean high water line. A waterfront block*, waterfront public park* or waterfront zoning lot* is a block, public park or zoning lot in the waterfront area that is adjacent to or intersected by the shoreline.

Most developments at the water's edge must provide public open space along it, with design and operational standards. Small lots, low-density residences and heavy manufacturing uses are exempt. Rules are in Article VI, Chapter 2.

A waterfront public access area (WPAA) is the portion of a waterfront zoning lot where publicly accessible open space is provided to and along the shoreline. All WPAAs are required to be improved with landscaping and trees, seating and other amenities. WPAAs can include a shore public walkway, an upland connection, a supplemental public access area, a public access area on a pier or floating structure, or any additional area improved for public use. The minimum amount of waterfront public access area required is a specified percentage for the zoning lot. A shore public walkway* is a linear public access area running alongside the shore. An upland connection* is a pedestrian way between a public place (a street, a sidewalk or a park, for example) and a shore public walkway. Upland connections may be provided along a private road. A supplemental public access area* is a public access area required in order to fulfill the minimum percentage of WPAA required on a waterfront zoning lot, once a shore public walkway and upland connection have been provided.

A waterfront yard is the portion of a waterfront zoning lot extending along the entire length of the shoreline which must be open and unobstructed from the lowest level to the sky, except for certain permitted obstructions. Depending upon the zoning district, the minimum depth is typically 30 to 40 feet. Shore public walkways are required to be located within the waterfront yard.

terms.term: WIE (Written in Error Failure to Maintain)
terms.def: Written in Error Failure to Maintain: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

terms.term: Window guards and approved limiting devices
terms.def: Approved guards or devices installed on windows to prevent children from falling. Owners must install them where a child 10 or younger lives or when a tenant asks in writing, leaving no more than four and a half inches of unguarded open space.
Legally required windows are mandated in dwelling units to provide necessary light, air and ventilation. Legally required windows cannot be located on or closer than 30 feet to a lot line.

A structure that keeps soil away from openings in foundation walls, allows proper grading and drainage, and lets sunlight into a below-grade room (basement) that would otherwise need artificial light.
The bill's sponsor took it out of consideration, so it will not move forward.

Issued to a licensed contractor after plan approval so construction can begin. DOB licenses many trades and only a registered contractor can do the work; licenses, registrations and certifications aim to keep unqualified people from endangering the public.
The kind of work on a building, such as plumbing or electrical, that must be shown on DOB work permits.
A program that repays workers for damages and lost wages from work-related injuries. Generally, employers must provide it to all workers, with some exceptions.
Work: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
Work Without a Permit: an abbreviation used on DOB violations and OATH summonses, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

A test by an EPA-certified inspector or risk assessor using an X-ray fluorescence analyzer to measure the lead content of all paint in an apartment. All rental units had to be tested by August 9, 2025, and results must be given to tenants.

A yard is a required open area along the lot lines of a zoning lot which must be unobstructed from the lowest level to the sky, except for certain permitted obstructions. Yard regulations ensure light and air between structures. A front yard* extends along the full width of a front lot line. In the case of a corner lot, any yard extending along the full length of a street line is considered a front yard. (See also Setbacks, Front Yard or Ground Level) A rear yard* extends for the full width of a rear lot line. In residential districts, the minimum depth of a rear yard is 30 feet, except in R2X districts. In commercial, manufacturing and R2X districts, the minimum depth of a rear yard is 20 feet. A corner lot is not required to have a rear yard. In commercial and manufacturing districts, and for some community facility buildings in residence districts, the rear yard may be occupied entirely by a single-story building up to a height of 23 feet. A rear yard equivalent* is an open area on a through lot required to comply with rear yard regulations. A side yard* extends along a side lot line from the required front yard, or from the front lot line if no front yard is required, to the required rear yard, or to the rear lot line if no rear yard is required. In the case of a corner lot, any yard that is not a front yard is considered a side yard.
Zoning: a DOB permit type code, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.
The City's online zoning and land use map. It shows zoning districts, special districts, (E) designations and rezonings, but is not the official zoning map; the "paper" pdf maps control.

The system of district-based rules that regulates land use and development across New York City. Zoning determines what can be built, how large, and for what purpose on any given lot. The NYC Zoning Resolution has been in place since 1961, built on the foundation of the 1916 resolution.

A zoning district is a residential, commercial or manufacturing area of the city within which zoning regulations govern land use and building bulk. Special purpose zoning districts have distinctive qualities where regulations are tailored to the neighborhood. Zoning districts are shown on the zoning maps.

The Department of Buildings checks plans for compliance with the Construction Codes and the Zoning Resolution before issuing a building permit, and is responsible for ongoing enforcement of zoning, including inspecting and issuing zoning violations.
DCP's service for zoning questions: call 212-720-3291 or submit an inquiry form on DCP's website; a zoning specialist responds within two business days.

The unit of land to which zoning regulations apply. A zoning lot may consist of one or more tax lots. FAR, coverage, and other bulk controls are calculated based on the zoning lot, not individual tax lots.

Combining two or more adjacent zoning lots into one larger lot, so buildable floor area can shift around the merged lot as-of-right. The merged lot must follow all bulk rules. Mergers often preserve older buildings by moving their unused floor area next door.

The map portion of the Zoning Resolution: 126 individual maps on a grid of 35 numbered sections, most divided into "a" through "d" sub-maps (for example 8D or 13B). The official "paper" maps (in pdf form) control; ZoLa is not the official zoning map. Each map notes its most recent rezoning and ULURP number.
A change to the official NYC Zoning Map, changing a district's boundaries or classification. Commonly called a rezoning. Goes through ULURP and requires City Council approval.

The 126 New York City zoning maps indicate the location and boundaries of zoning districts and are part of the Zoning Resolution. Each map covers a land area of approximately 8,000 feet (north/south) by 12,500 feet (east/west). Zoning map amendments, or rezonings, are subject to ULURP review. *Words and phrases followed by an asterisk (*) are defined terms in the Zoning Resolution, primarily in Section 12-10. Consult the Zoning Resolution for the official and legally binding definitions of these words and phrases.

The law that contains New York City's zoning regulations. It has a map portion showing where every zoning district applies and a text portion containing all the rules, organized into 14 Articles plus Appendices. The current Resolution took effect on December 15, 1961.

The text portion of the Zoning Resolution containing all the rules, organized into 14 Articles (numbered with Roman numerals), each divided into up to nine chapters, then sections. Articles II, III and IV set baseline rules for Residence, Commercial and Manufacturing Districts. There is no printed version; DCP stopped printing it in 2017.

A change to the text of the NYC Zoning Resolution itself, as opposed to a map change. Text amendments can apply citywide or be limited to specific areas. They go through ULURP and require City Council approval.

Zoning promotes orderly development and separates incompatible uses, such as industrial and residential. The Zoning Resolution is the legal instrument that regulates land use and limits building size, shape, height and setback.
Zoning Regulations: an abbreviation DOB uses for a law, code or policy document, per the DOB Acronym Glossary.

rules.what: If a space with a non-conforming use stays vacant for more than two years, only conforming uses may occupy it. Small older shops in Residence Districts are exempt: new retail, service or office uses can re-occupy them at any time.
New apartment buildings with nine or more units must provide recreation space equal to three percent of residential floor area, indoors or outdoors, accessible to all residents.

New multi-family residential buildings must provide one enclosed bicycle parking space for every two dwelling units; commercial and community facility uses calculate requirements by size, and small establishments may waive out.

Zoning's typical required rear yard depth is 20 feet, applying in all districts for all building types, increased for narrow lots and upper parts of tall residential buildings, reduced for shallow lots, and not required on corner lots or full-block sites.
After damage or demolition, a non-complying building may be reconstructed if at least 25 percent of the building remains standing; more lenient rules apply to single- and two-family homes.

Most new buildings must provide street trees along the sidewalk; in low-density Residence Districts a planting strip along the curb is also required, and in Residence Districts planting is required between the building and the front property line. Parks can exempt sites where sidewalk planting is not possible.

On properties with an (E) designation, the Office of Environmental Remediation must confirm the project includes required hazardous materials, noise or air quality mitigations before DOB can issue construction permits.

Projects using MIH or UAP must work with HPD on an affordable housing plan before DOB issues construction permits, and HPD must sign off on finished units before DOB issues a certificate of occupancy.

rules.rule: Store size in neighborhood commercial districts
rules.what: Clothing and department stores cannot exceed 10,000 square feet in neighborhood commercial districts; the limit applies per business, not to the total on the lot.

rules.rule: Commercial uses in neighborhood commercial districts
rules.what: In neighborhood commercial districts, commercial uses are limited to the lower two stories of a building, with added access and nuisance controls where commercial and residential uses share the second story.

rules.rule: Sign size in C1 and C2 districts
rules.what: In C1 or C2 neighborhood commercial districts, a sign may equal three times the street frontage, up to a maximum of 150 square feet; each storefront calculates from its own frontage.
Most developments at the water's edge must provide public open space along it, meeting design and operational requirements; small lots, low-density residences and heavy manufacturing uses are exempt.
Work generally needs a DOB permit. Some minor alterations, ordinary repairs, and replacing faucets, toilets and sinks need no permit and may be done by someone without a license (AC 28-105.4).
rules.penalty: Violations, court appearances, and civil/criminal penalties

rules.what: A project cannot begin until its plans are approved by a DOB Plan Examiner, or accepted if Professionally Certified; objections on disapproved applications must be resolved first.
After plan approval, a work permit is issued to a licensed contractor; only a registered contractor can perform the work.
When permitted work is finished it must be inspected for final sign-off and a work completion notification submitted to DOB.
Required for major buildings, including new buildings, alterations and demolitions 10 stories or more, and facade work on buildings 15 stories or more (BC 3310, AC 28-110.1).
Commissioning is mandatory when permitted equipment exceeds a total heating capacity of 600 kBTU/h.

Spaces where 75 or more people gather need a Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation (PACO). The initial PACO, issued after DOB inspection, lasts one year; renewal requires an annual FDNY inspection (FC 105.6).
Architectural details may project no more than three inches into the public right of way as-of-right under the Building Code.
A sidewalk that differs from DOT's standard material, color, scoring or dimensions requires Public Design Commission approval.

Storm water from all water-resistant surfaces on a property must drain into a public storm or combined sewer, or an on-site private system such as a drywell; sidewalk and roadway runoff along the frontage must go to a street drainage system.
Excavation work requires coordination with FDNY.
Where the Zoning Resolution is modified by BSA, an approved BSA resolution with BSA-stamped plans is required before DOB review proceeds (ZR 72-00).

rules.rule: Loft Law work in IMD buildings
rules.what: Owners must get a Letter of No Objection from the Loft Board before a permit for work not directly related to IMD units, and Loft Board certification before a permit for work to legalize IMD units.
Occupants may not exceed the number on the Certificate of Occupancy or allowed by BC 1004.1; FDNY may act where crowding or blocked exits threaten safety.
Building owners must provide heat from October 1 to May 31.

During heat season, from 6am to 10pm, when the outside temperature is below 55 degrees Fahrenheit, owners must heat apartments to at least 68 degrees Fahrenheit. HPD can only issue a violation if it is below 55 degrees outside at the time of inspection.
During heat season, from 10pm to 6am, owners must heat apartments to at least 62 degrees Fahrenheit regardless of the outside temperature. Heat is not required in kitchens or bathrooms.
Owners must provide hot water 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, at a constant minimum temperature of 120 degrees Fahrenheit.

rules.rule: Heat and hot water violation penalties
rules.what: Heat and hot water violations are Class C and must be corrected immediately. They are posted at the building at inspection.
rules.penalty: $250 to $500 per day per violation from the day the notice is posted until corrected; $500 to $1,000 per day for each later violation at the same building within two consecutive calendar years (hot water) or two consecutive October 1 to May 31 periods (heat).

rules.what: Owners must notify tenants in writing in advance of the day and time they need access to inspect or make required repairs. Appointments must be between 9am and 5pm, Monday through Friday, unless the tenant agrees otherwise. No notice is needed for urgent repairs such as gas or water leaks, stopped drains, leaking roofs, or dangerous ceilings. Workers must show they are authorized by the owner.

Tenants may not damage the building, are responsible for their guests, must answer the owner's annual window guard and lead paint inquiries, must maintain smoke and CO detectors, must obey legal lease terms, pay rent on time, respect other tenants, and allow access for required inspections and repairs.

Owners must keep apartments and common areas safe and maintained under the Housing Maintenance Code and Multiple Dwelling Law, including security, heat, hot and cold water and good lighting; fix leaks, mold and pests immediately and inspect for them yearly; provide smoke and CO detectors and fire egress; and keep records of lead paint, mold and self-closing door compliance.
Owners may rent only legal residential space for living, as defined by the property's Certificate of Occupancy.
Owners must post a notice in the building's common area about the availability of the ABCs of Housing (Housing Information Guide notice).
rules.penalty: Class A: $250 for each failure to post the housing information guide notice.

rules.what: Owners of buildings with three or more units, and of 1-2 family homes where neither the owner nor immediate family lives, must register annually with HPD at nyc.gov/propertyregistration (registration period June 1 to August 31).
rules.penalty: An unregistered owner cannot certify correction of HPD violations, request dismissal of violations, or bring any case against tenants in Housing Court, including evictions.

rules.what: Owners of rent-stabilized and rent-controlled apartments must register rents with HCR every year, online between April 1 and July 31.

Owners must offer rent-stabilized tenants a renewal lease of one or two years (tenant's choice) at the Rent Guidelines Board rate, on a DHCR Renewal Lease Form by mail or personal delivery no more than 150 and no less than 90 days before the lease expires. The owner must return the fully signed copy within 30 days. Renewals may not be retroactive.
A rent-stabilized tenant has 60 days after the renewal offer to choose a term, sign, and return the lease.
rules.penalty: If the tenant does not accept within 60 days, the owner may refuse to renew and may go to court to evict after the current lease ends.

rules.what: All apartment doors and doors in and leading to public halls must be self-closing. Tenants must not block, prop, tape, wedge or override them. Owners must fix a self-closing door violation within 14 days and tenants must give access; HPD reinspects within 20 days of the deadline and may fix the door through the Emergency Repair Program.
rules.penalty: Class C: buildings with 5 or fewer units, $50 per violation per day; more than 5 units, $50 to $150 per violation plus $125 per violation per day.

rules.what: If you suspect a gas leak, open nearby doors and windows and leave immediately without using electrical switches, flames or phones in the building; call 911 from a safe distance, then call the gas provider. Gas restoration must always be done by a licensed plumber and may require access to all apartments.

Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors are required in every apartment in buildings with three or more units and in 1-2 family homes that are not owner-occupied. Owners must install smoke detectors in each apartment.
rules.penalty: Missing or defective detector violations must be corrected within 30 days.

rules.what: Owners must install at least one approved CO detector in each unit, within 15 feet of the main entrance to each sleeping room, with an audible end-of-useful-life alarm, and give tenants written information on testing and maintenance.

Tenants must maintain smoke and CO detectors: test them at least once a month, replace batteries at least twice a year (immediately when the low-battery alarm sounds), use the recommended batteries, and never paint over them. A tenant who removed a detector or let the battery die must restore it.
rules.penalty: Owners may charge a legally prescribed fee to replace a device that was lost, damaged or not maintained.

rules.what: Owners of tenant-occupied multiple dwellings must provide stove knob covers or locking stove knobs for gas stoves where they know or should know a child under six lives, and in any unit on request, unless no compatible device exists. Tenants may refuse in writing. Owners must send an annual notice about this obligation each January.
Double cylinder door locks and key-locked window gates that need a key to exit are illegal and must be removed.
rules.penalty: Must be corrected within 24 hours.

rules.what: Owners must post a Fire Safety Notice on the inside of every apartment entrance door and in common areas, and distribute it to each unit, to new tenants, and annually during fire prevention week.
Fire escapes and sprinkler systems must be maintained in proper working order.

Owners of apartment buildings must prepare and distribute the FDNY fire and non-fire emergency preparedness guide and annual bulletin (deadline January 29), including at lease signing, and post Close the Door notices when bulletins go out.

Owners of pre-1960 buildings must ask tenants in writing, at lease signing and every year on the annual notice form, whether a child under six lives in or routinely spends 10 or more hours a week in the apartment. The annual notice goes out January 1-16 to February 15; tenant responses are due February 15; owners must investigate units that did not respond from February 16 through March.

Tenants must fill out and return the annual lead paint notice each January, and notify the owner in writing if a child under six comes to live with them or routinely spends 10 or more hours a week there.

Where a child under six lives or spends 10 or more hours a week, owners must visually inspect the apartment and common areas for lead paint hazards at least once a year and give the results to the tenant.

Any deteriorated or peeling paint, and any work disturbing paint in a building covered by Local Law 1, must be handled by appropriately certified contractors using safe work practices, followed by a clearance test by a separate independent certified contractor.
When an apartment changes tenants, owners must complete Local Law 1 turnover work using certified contractors before the new tenant moves in, whether or not the new tenant has a child.
rules.penalty: Turnover violations apply to all window and door friction surfaces in the apartment.

rules.what: All rental units had to be tested for lead paint by an EPA-certified inspector or risk assessor using an XRF analyzer by August 9, 2025. If a child under six moves in or routinely spends 10 or more hours a week there, testing must be done within one year or by August 9, 2025, whichever is sooner. Results must be given to tenants.
rules.penalty: HPD may audit records; missing records may result in a violation.

rules.what: Owners must keep all lead-based paint compliance records for 10 years.
rules.penalty: Significant civil penalties for failing to keep these documents.

rules.what: Lead-based paint hazard violations are Class C and must be corrected within 21 days by trained, certified workers using safe work practices.
rules.penalty: Orders 614, 616, 617: $250 per day per violation up to $10,000; Order 618: up to $1,000; Order 619: up to $1,500 per violation; Order 620: $1,000 to $5,000 per violation; criminal misdemeanor punishable by a fine up to $500, up to six months in jail, or both.

rules.what: In buildings built before 1978, federal law requires safe work practices whenever paint not known to be lead-free is disturbed; Local Law 1 adds requirements for pre-1960 buildings with a child under 6 and 1960 to 1978 buildings known to have lead paint. Contractors must affirm compliance on all such permit applications and, where applicable, file a Notice of Commencement with DOHMH.
rules.penalty: Fines of up to $2,000.

rules.what: Owners of multiple dwellings must inspect units for mold every year (January), respond to complaints from tenants or HPD, fix leaks promptly, and thoroughly clean mold from vacant apartments before a new tenant moves in.

When violations are issued in buildings with 10 or more units and there is over 10 square feet of mold, licensed assessors and remediators must be used; otherwise specific safe work practices apply. (The tenant guide states this as buildings with more than 10 units.) Mold violations must be corrected within 21 days.
rules.penalty: Additional DEP penalties if remediation is done without required professionals; Class C mold penalties: 5 or fewer units, $50 per violation per day; more than 5 units, $50 to $150 per violation plus $125 per violation per day.

rules.what: Owners must give each tenant, with the lease, the What Tenants and Landlords Should Know About Indoor Allergens and Local Law 55 fact sheet and a notice of the owner's duty to keep the building free of indoor allergens.

Owners of buildings selected for the Underlying Conditions Program must have a professional investigate the cause of leaks or mold affecting multiple apartments and fix the conditions and related violations within four months.

Owners of buildings with three or more apartments must send an annual window guard notice (January) and install approved window guards or limiting devices on all windows in apartments where a child 10 or younger lives (including first-floor bathrooms and windows onto balconies or terraces) and in common areas, and in any apartment where the tenant asks in writing. No more than four and a half inches of unguarded open space is allowed.
rules.penalty: Missing or defective window guards must be corrected within 21 days; Class C penalties: 5 or fewer units, $50 per violation per day; more than 5 units, $50 to $150 per violation plus $125 per violation per day.

rules.what: Tenants must not remove or unscrew window guards or limiting devices for any reason, including to install air conditioners.

Owners must hire only pest control professionals licensed by the NY State Department of Environmental Conservation to treat apartments. Mice, roach and rat violations must be corrected within 21 days.
rules.penalty: Class C penalties: 5 or fewer units, $50 per violation per day; more than 5 units, $50 to $150 per violation plus $125 per violation per day.

rules.what: Owners must report bedbug occurrences in their buildings to HPD each year between December 1 and December 31. Individual or joint owners may use the paper form; all others must file electronically. The filing receipt must be provided to tenants.

Owners must provide tenants and post the notices HPD and FDNY require, including the Housing Information Guide notice, Gas Leak Notice, Fire Safety Notice, Shut the Door signs, certificate of inspection visits, garbage collection sign, name and location of the person with boiler room keys, floor signs, street number, janitor name and address, smoke and CO detector notices, maximum room occupancy, bedbug filing receipt, property registration number, and as needed Notice of Interruption of Services, Safe Construction Bill of Rights and disaster response signage. Owners should check signage each September.

Owners must correct HPD violations within these times: lead-based paint hazard 21 days; window guard 21 days; smoke detector 30 days; CO detector 30 days; double cylinder lock 24 hours; illegal window gate 24 hours; mold (over 100 sq ft in buildings with 10 or more units) 21 days; mice, roaches or rats 21 days; self-closing doors 14 days.
Owners have 90 days from notice to correct a Class A (non-hazardous) violation before civil penalties begin.
rules.penalty: Example: $250 for each failure to post the housing information guide notice.

rules.what: Owners have 30 days from notice to correct a Class B (hazardous) violation before civil penalties begin.
rules.penalty: $25 to $100 per violation, plus $10 per violation per day.

rules.what: Owners have 24 hours to correct Class C (immediately hazardous) violations not otherwise listed (not heat, hot water, illegal devices or lead paint). If the owner does not, HPD may make the repair through the Emergency Repair Program, usually within 24 hours for most Class C violations.
rules.penalty: 5 or fewer units: $50 per violation per day; more than 5 units: $50 to $150 per violation plus $125 per violation per day.

rules.what: Once a violation is fixed, the owner must certify the correction to HPD through eCertification or the mailed forms. HPD has 70 days to try to reinspect and must attempt reinspection for lead paint and self-closing door certifications. If unconfirmed, the violation closes after 70 days on the owner's certification, except lead paint, which HPD must observe.
rules.penalty: If reinspection finds the condition was not fixed, the owner is subject to penalties and the case may be referred to HPD's Housing Litigation Division.

rules.what: When HPD makes emergency repairs, the cost plus fees is billed to the property through the Department of Finance.
rules.penalty: Unpaid charges become a tax lien on the property that bears interest.

rules.what: Owners of buildings selected for the Heat Sensors Program (50 per year, selected in July) must install internet-capable heat sensors in each unit.
Owners of buildings in the CoNH program must obtain a Certificate of No Harassment from HPD before DOB approves certain permits involving demolition or a change in use or occupancy.
rules.penalty: If tenants are found to have been harassed, the owner cannot obtain the certificate.

rules.what: Owners may not harass tenants to force them out or give up their rights, and may not lock tenants out. Tenants may bring a case in Housing Court or to HCR.

Owners who sign a buyout agreement with a lawful occupant must report its terms to HPD by email at buyoutagreement@hpd.nyc.gov (Local Law 102 of 2019). Buyout offers may not involve threats, obscene language, false information, or contact at the tenant's workplace without written permission.
rules.penalty: Violating buyout rules can lead to a tenant lawsuit in Housing Court.

rules.what: The only legal way to evict for unpaid rent is a non-payment proceeding in Housing Court. The owner must notify the tenant that rent is late, the balance, and that eviction will follow if unpaid; three days after notice or an oral demand, the owner may file. Evictions require a judgment of possession and a warrant directing a City marshal.
Before starting a holdover eviction case, the owner must serve a preliminary notice ending the lease. For a nuisance case, the owner must prove the conduct is persistent and egregious.

Owners, brokers, managers and agents may not deny housing based on race, color, religion, national origin, gender, gender identity, sexual orientation, age, marital or partnership status, family status or children, disability, alienage or citizenship, military status, domestic violence victim status, lawful occupation, or lawful source of income. Complaints must be filed with CCHR within one year of the last act.

Owners must let tenant organizations meet free of charge in any community or social room in the building, even if the room normally has a fee. Meetings must be at reasonable times and peaceful, without blocking access. Owners may not harass or retaliate against tenants for organizing.
Except for service animals used by blind, deaf or disabled people, pets are allowed at the owner's discretion, usually stated in the lease. Many animals cannot legally be kept as pets in NYC.
rules.penalty: Keeping a pet without permission may be a serious lease violation and grounds to end the tenancy.

rules.what: Owners of multiple dwellings using keyless smart access systems must give tenants a data retention and privacy policy, secure the data, limit retention, and not use the system to track tenants to harass or evict them, track relationship status, collect data from non-tenants, or share a minor's data without parental permission.
rules.penalty: Tenants have a private right of action for unlawful sale of data.

rules.what: Owners, managers or superintendents should immediately repair broken locks and intercoms to secure buildings; tenants can report them to 311.

When doing construction in a residential building, owners must file applications and get DOB permits, give tenants proper notice, and keep required exits, structural elements and fire protection devices maintained at all times. Exits may not be blocked, fire-rated material protecting occupied apartments may not be left removed during non-work hours, and fire protection systems may not be compromised except as the Fire Code allows.
rules.penalty: Violations range from $500 to $10,000; agencies may order a fire guard, generally about $750 to $1,250 per 24 hours.

rules.what: Owners must give tenants notice if essential services will be out for more than two hours.

Owners of multiple dwellings applying for a permit for work beyond minor alterations or ordinary repairs must distribute and post a Safe Construction Bill of Rights, and give each occupied unit and post a Tenant Protection Plan notice (Administrative Code section 120.1.3) until the work is done, in English and as necessary in Spanish, Arabic, Haitian Creole, Chinese, Korean and Russian.
If fire protection or safety systems will be compromised during asbestos abatement, the owner must file a Workplace Safety Plan with DEP and get an A-TRU permit.

Starting in 2024, most buildings over 25,000 square feet must stay within annual greenhouse gas emissions limits under Local Law 97. Affordable and rent-regulated buildings are covered but treated differently.
rules.penalty: Buildings over their annual limits face financial penalties.

rules.what: Under the NYC Administrative Code, property owners are generally responsible for installing, maintaining and repairing the sidewalk adjacent to their property, including the intersection quadrant for a corner property. For 1, 2 and 3 family homes, the City may make the repairs if the owner fails to and will charge the owner. Owners are not charged for repairs of defects solely related to street trees.
rules.penalty: For 1, 2 and 3 family homes, the City may make repairs the owner fails to make and charge the owner.

rules.what: Parks maintains tree beds for the first two years after planting; after two years, property owners are responsible for tree-bed maintenance.

Residential property owners are responsible for making sure trash, recycling and compost (food scraps and yard waste) are set out correctly. Fines apply per violation and can increase with each violation within a 12-month period.
rules.penalty: Fines per violation, increasing with each violation within 12 months

rules.what: Single- and two-family homes and buildings with up to 9 residential units may set out trash after 6:00 PM, in a bin.
rules.penalty: $50 first offense, $100 second, $200 third and subsequent

rules.what: Buildings with 10 or more residential units may set out trash after 6:00 PM in a bin of 55 gallons or less with a secure lid, or after 8:00 PM if bags are placed directly on the curb.
rules.penalty: $50 first offense, $100 second, $200 third and subsequent

rules.what: All waste should be set out by midnight to ensure collection, unless specified otherwise.
As of November 12, 2024, single- and two-family homes and buildings with up to 9 units must set out trash in bins of 55 gallons or less with secure lids.
rules.penalty: $50 first offense, $100 second, $200 third and subsequent

rules.rule: Official NYC Bins required for trash, 1 to 9 units
rules.what: As of June 1, 2026, properties with 1 to 9 residential units (and special-use buildings that get DSNY collection, such as City agencies, nonprofits, houses of worship and professional offices in residential buildings) must set out trash only in official NYC Bins. A warning period ran through September 7, 2026; full enforcement began Tuesday, September 8, 2026.
rules.penalty: $50 first offense, $100 second, $200 third and subsequent

rules.what: Properties with 31 or more residential units must use Empire Bins for trash; properties with 10 to 30 units may choose Empire Bins or official NYC Bins. In BK2 (Brooklyn Community District 2), 31+ unit properties had to register (registration ran July 1 to 31) and 10 to 30 unit properties could opt in. Empire Bins take only bagged trash, not recycling or compost; bags may not be left outside the bins.
Bins must close fully to contain waste and keep pests out, and owners must have enough bins for all trash and compost. Overflowing, broken or uncovered bins, or waste spilling out, may be fined.
rules.penalty: $50 first offense, $100 second, $200 third and subsequent

rules.what: Store bins inside, in alleyways, courtyards or other outdoor areas away from public sidewalks. If there is no space, bins may be stored within three feet of the building, kept neat, and must allow pedestrian travel. Sidewalk enclosures are subject to NYC DOT regulations.
All NYC residents and businesses must recycle. Not separating recycling and compost from trash, or setting them out incorrectly, may be fined.
rules.penalty: Fines may apply

rules.what: Recycling bins must be clearly labeled, hold 55 gallons or less and have a secure lid. Recycling in bags must use clear plastic bags. Cardboard boxes cannot be used as bins.
rules.penalty: $50 first offense, $100 second, $200 third and subsequent

rules.what: Put recycling at the curb after 6:00 PM in a labeled bin of 55 gallons or less with a secure lid, or after 8:00 PM in a clear plastic bag. All recycling must be out by midnight.

Separate metal, glass jars and bottles, rigid plastics and cartons from trash and set them out together in a labeled bin with a secure lid or in a clear plastic bag. Empty and rinse containers. Cartons go with metal, glass and plastic, not with paper. Tape large glass items and double-bag broken glass.
Separate mixed paper and cardboard from trash and set out in a labeled bin with a secure lid or a clear plastic bag. Cardboard may be flattened, tied with twine and set out next to bins or bags.

Owners or managers of buildings with 4 or more residential units must designate at least one recycling storage area that is reasonably accessible to residents, has enough bins to separate materials and prevent overflow, and displays recycling signage with clearly labeled bins.
rules.penalty: Fines that increase with each new offense (amounts not stated)

rules.what: As of April 1, 2025, separating compost (leaf and yard waste, food scraps and food-soiled paper) from trash is mandatory citywide for all NYC residents.

Set out leaf and yard waste, food scraps and food-soiled paper in labeled bins of 55 gallons or less with secure lids, or in DSNY brown compost bins. Bins may be lined with clear, paper or compostable bags (no black plastic bags). Extra yard waste may go in paper lawn and leaf bags or clear plastic bags; twigs and branches may be bundled with twine.
Compost is collected weekly on your recycling day.
Owners and managers of buildings with 4 or more units must provide a designated storage area with clearly labeled compost bins.

Bundles of twigs and branches can be no larger than 2 feet by 4 feet and no heavier than 40 pounds, tied with twine or rope (no nylon line or tape), with nails removed. Set out on your Curbside Composting day; where that service is not available, set out with large items on your trash-only day.
Remove all lights, ornaments, tinsel and metal or plastic stands, and set the tree out unbagged for Curbside Composting collection. Wreath frames and wires go with recycling.
Commercial landscapers may not leave yard waste for DSNY collection; it must go to a permitted composting facility.
Mattresses and box springs must be fully enclosed in a clear plastic bag sealed securely to prevent the spread of bed bugs. Set them out on your trash-only day, not your recycling day.
rules.penalty: $50 first offense, $100 second, $200 third and subsequent (the furniture page states improper disposal can bring a fine of up to $300)

rules.what: Residents get free curbside removal of large items. Set out up to 6 large items per collection day; no appointment is needed (appointments are no longer offered). Mostly metal or rigid plastic items go out with recycling; all other large items go out on your trash-only day, not your recycling day.
rules.penalty: Items with special disposal rules not followed may be refused and fined (amount not stated)

rules.what: Take furniture apart when possible and bundle smaller pieces with tape or twine. Wood and wood composites are not recyclable and go out on trash-only day. Glass furniture, windows and mirrors go out with trash.
Roll rugs and carpets up, tie securely with twine and set out with trash.

Air conditioners, dehumidifiers, refrigerators, freezers and water and wine coolers need their CFC/Freon removed by trained DSNY personnel before collection; make an appointment for CFC removal. Removal is free except for appliances with R600a or R32 refrigerant. DSNY puts a sticker on the appliance after removal; leave it at the curb and it is collected with recycling.
DSNY cannot collect appliances with R600a or R32 refrigerant (marked by a yellow triangle sticker with black flames). Contact the manufacturer or a private carter.
Mostly metal or plastic small appliances go out with recycling. Remove rechargeable batteries first and dispose of them properly.

It is illegal to dispose of covered electronic devices (computers, monitors, TVs, printers, phones, tablets, game consoles and their cords, as listed under the NYS Electronic Equipment Recycling and Reuse Act) with trash or recycling. Use retail or nonprofit drop-off sites, Community E-Waste Events, Special Waste Drop-Off sites, SAFE Disposal events, manufacturer takeback, or ecycleNYC (for buildings with 10+ units).
Public litter baskets are for light trash from pedestrians only (dog waste only inside a tied bag). Household and commercial waste may not be put in or beside litter baskets.
rules.penalty: Up to $350

rules.what: It is illegal to leave trash on the sidewalk, street or any public space, throw it from windows or vehicles, or sweep or blow it into the street. Property owners must keep adjacent public areas (sidewalk including tree pits and grass strips, gutter, yards, alleys, air shafts) clean and litter-free. Waste that could scatter must be bundled or tied.
rules.penalty: Up to $400

rules.what: Owners must clean their sidewalk area, which extends 18 inches into the street (the gutter).
rules.penalty: $100 to $300 (NYC Admin Code 16-118(2))

rules.what: Owners, lessees, tenants and occupants must clear the sidewalk adjacent to their property: if snow stops between 7:00 AM and 4:49 PM, within 4 hours; between 5:00 PM and 8:59 PM, within 14 hours; between 9:00 PM and 6:59 AM, by 11:00 AM. Clear a path at least 4 feet wide where possible.
rules.penalty: 1st offense $100 to $150; 2nd $150 to $350; 3rd and subsequent $250 to $350

rules.what: Do not push snow into the street or onto crosswalks; move it to the yard, behind the stoop line or onto a grassy curb strip. Keep adjacent fire hydrants clear. Corner owners must clear a path to the crosswalk including pedestrian ramps. Residents must clear plow ridges in front of their driveways.
rules.penalty: $100 Notice of Violation for snow placed in the street

rules.what: Placing flyers or business cards on car or truck windows, or posting them on City property such as lampposts and traffic signs, is illegal.
Missed trash, recycling or compost pickups can be reported to 311 starting at 8:00 AM the day after your collection day.
Collection on recognized holidays is subject to change; check DSNY's site, social media, press releases or 311 when your collection day falls on a holiday.

rules.rule: Food Protection Certificate holder on site
rules.what: A worker holding a Health Department Food Protection Certificate must be present at all times while food is prepared or served at a food service establishment.
Every food service establishment must display its Health Department letter grade card.
A hand-wash-only sink is required in every bathroom and within 25 clear feet of any place a worker prepares or serves food.
Sinks for washing pots, pans and dishes must connect to special plumbing that captures grease before wastewater enters the sewer.
DEP requires grease interceptors (grease traps) for food service establishments and some other businesses.
An imminent health hazard found during a Health Department inspection must be corrected before the restaurant can reopen or receive a grade.
rules.penalty: Restaurant cannot reopen or be graded until corrected

rules.what: Some critical violations must be corrected before food can be served or a permit issued, and they may lower the letter grade.
rules.penalty: Lower letter grade

rules.what: Large commercial stoves require a range hood, which needs a special permit from the Fire Department.
Shared kitchen operators must be permitted by the Health Department.
Outdoor business signs that are electric or larger than a certain size require DOB permits.
Sidewalk awnings and canopies require a permit to install.
Any demolition, even part of an interior during a business remodel, requires a DOB work permit.
Building owners must control asbestos during renovations or other work by hiring special contractors.

Landmarks and buildings in historic districts require special permission from the Landmarks Preservation Commission to change; work that does not need a DOB permit needs a Certificate of Appropriateness, Minor Work or No Effect.
Under State law, employees must be paid an additional amount for time worked beyond 40 hours per week.
Under State law, employers must pay wages to an employee sent home early for lack of work.
Employees must be paid at least the minimum hourly wage set by City, State and federal law.
Employers must complete an Employment Eligibility Verification (I-9) for each person hired, proving they may legally work in the United States.
All employers must pay taxes into the unemployment insurance program.
Employers generally must provide workers' compensation insurance to all workers, with some exceptions.
Individuals must complete the Office of Child Support Enforcement form before applying for many NYC licenses and permits.
A business must have a State Liquor Authority license to serve alcohol.
A business must have a Certificate of Authority to collect sales tax on behalf of New York State.
